items.title: October 2026 Monthly Housing Trends: Buyers and Sellers Hit Pause as Rates Surge
items.description: October 2026 Monthly Housing Trends: Buyers and Sellers Hit Pause as Rates Surge By Jake Krimmel Nov 04, 2026 Market outlook If September’s slowdown hinted at a fall stall for the housing market, October confirmed it. Mortgage rates peaked at 7.40% in mid-October, capping a six-week 74 basis point surge. And although rates have since eased to 7.24%, the damage to purchasing power has been done. The same monthly principal and interest payment now supports a loan nearly 6% smaller than it did in late August. The October Realtor.com® data show a market where almost everyone has pressed pause for now. Buyers on the sidelines are staying there, and sellers – whether they’re on or off market – are disengaging as well. New listings fell at their fastest rate in three years, while current sellers are not slashing prices or pulling listings at meaningfully higher rates than last year, when falling mortgage rates kept the market unseasonably warm. What happens next depends on the broader economy. A dip in the 10-year Treasury yield could restore some purchasing power, but it could also tempt buyers to wait for further progress. Our base case is that mortgage rates remain above 7% in the near term, with the market facing an early chill as winter approaches. In This Report Top storylines and key questions Core metrics: October 2026 Summary tables Data appendix October’s top storylines, according to the data Buyers pull back, as they battle mortgage rates and loss of purchasing power Pending sales are down 10.5% year over year, the steepest annual decline since October 2023, and contract signings are also down 17%. With 30-year rates averaging 7.33% in October, 107 basis points above a year ago, buyers have lost real purchasing power. Sellers freeze rather than panic New listings fell 7.5% year over year, the steepest drop since September 2023, but delistings and price cuts are moving sideways. About 4.4% of active listings were delisted, versus 4.6% a year ago, and the share with a price cut (20.5%) is just 0.2 points above last year and down from September. Sellers are disengaging rather than showing signs of real distress. About 43% of current active listings have ever had their price reduced, down from nearly 55% a year ago. Inventory growth accelerates for fourth straight month, closest to pre-pandemic norm yet Active listings grew 7.4% year over year, topping 1.18 million homes for sale, the fourth straight month of faster growth. National inventory sits 6.7% below pre-pandemic norms, the narrowest gap we have seen yet. Key questions Q: Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, the highest since 2023. Where is that showing up in the market, and is the impact the same everywhere? A: Even with rates dipping slightly in the latest reading (7.24% on Oct 29, down from 7.40% in mid-October), 30-year rates are still 107 basis points above this time last year and 53 above the start of September. That loss of purchasing power (a 10.4% loss compared to a year ago and a 5.2% loss since the start of September) is showing up first in the demand indicators. The stock of homes under contract is down about 10.5% year over year, contract signings are down by 17%, and mortgage applications for purchase are down more than 18% from a year ago over the past two weeks. Q: Last month, we said sellers were the thing to watch. Are they responding to weaker demand by cutting prices, pulling listings, or sitting out altogether? A: Right now it looks more like a seller pause than an exodus. For the fourth consecutive month, more than 1 in 5 listings saw a price cut, but the share is only 0.2 points above last year and slipped from September. New listings are down year over year at a time of year when they are already seasonally low. Sellers know this is a poor time to list, and you do not list into weak demand unless you need to. What we have not seen is a meaningful increase in delistings. That matters for two reasons. First, sellers are not giving up yet. And second, we also need to reframe the delisting conversation this time of year, because a higher count, even if it were happening, would not signal seller stress as we approach the holidays. A seller throwing in the towel in July is different from one calling it quits around Halloween or nearing Thanksgiving. Q: What should we be monitoring heading into the holiday months as 2026 comes to a close? A: Prices vs. inventory. More inventory and slower sales mean rising months of supply, but if sellers are not cutting prices more deeply, the market may not be getting as buyer-friendly as the inventory numbers imply. List prices are down 2.2%, the 12th straight year-over-year decline, but with mortgage rates still significantly higher than this time last year, potential buyers are still operating at a loss when it comes to purchasing power. The Realtor.com ® 2026Q3 Market Clock® Report found the US housing market is on the cusp of buyer’s market territory, and about two-thirds of the 100 largest metros were either outright buyer’s markets or trending in that direction. Still, buyers gaining ground at the negotiating table is different from gaining enough purchasing power to pull would-be buyers off the sidelines. Until the affordability math shifts notably, do not expect swings in housing demand. items.title: What housing market headlines can't tell your clients
items.description: Mortgage rates are moving closer to 7%, and housing demand is showing signs of stabilizing. But what does that mean for a homeowner preparing to list, a buyer wondering whether to wait or an agent trying to set realistic expectations? In his latest Housing Market Tracker , HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami explains why a path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table. While weekly pending home sales have recently stabilized, that doesn't yet signal a sustained recovery. For housing professionals, the opportunity is to translate those national trends into what clients are experiencing in their own markets. HousingWire Data from Houston, Phoenix and Tampa reveals three things worth watching: Look beyond the headline. A national or regional trend may not reflect the competition your client faces. Watch how the signals move together. Changes in pending sales, inventory and price reductions can reveal where competition may be heading. Recognize when conditions are shifting. Recent market activity can change before the longer-term numbers tell the same story. Look beyond the headline A client sees that housing demand is stabilizing and asks whether it's finally a good time to sell. Houston demonstrates why the answer requires more local context. Across the Houston metro, the ratio of new pending sales to new listings improved during October, but not because buyer activity increased. New listings declined faster than pending sales, making the ratio look stronger even as fewer homes went under contract. Within Houston city limits, the opposite happened. Pending sales declined faster than new listings, pushing the ratio lower. Even inventory told a different story. Active inventory was higher than a year ago across the metro but lower within the city. Neither market showed growing pending activity, yet the conditions affecting buyers and sellers were different. For a homeowner, that distinction matters more than whether a regional headline describes the market as improving. The takeaway: Use broader housing trends to start the conversation, then show clients what's happening among the homes they're actually competing with. A seller needs to understand current competition and buyer activity, not simply whether the overall market appears stronger. Watch how the signals move together A homeowner considering whether to wait for lower mortgage rates might assume that more affordable financing will bring more buyers. But lower rates could also encourage more sellers to list, making the relationship between supply and demand especially important. Phoenix illustrates what happens when several indicators point in the same direction. Over the latest four-week period, new pending sales declined faster than new listings. Compared with a year ago, pending activity was down nearly 17%, while new listings were slightly higher. Meanwhile, active inventory continued to grow, and more than half of active listings had experienced a price reduction. Together, those indicators suggest increasing competition among sellers. Fewer homes are moving into pending status, more inventory is available and price reductions are becoming more prevalent. That doesn't guarantee prices will fall, but it identifies conditions that could create additional pricing pressure if the trend continues. The takeaway: Don't evaluate pending sales, inventory or price reductions in isolation. When several indicators reinforce one another, they provide stronger evidence of where conditions may be headed. That can help sellers evaluate pricing and timing, while giving buyers a clearer picture of their negotiating position. Recognize when conditions are shifting A seller points out that inventory is still lower than last year. Does that mean competition remains limited? Tampa shows why the direction of recent activity matters just as much as the year-over-year comparison. Within Tampa city limits, new listings and pending sales were essentially unchanged over the latest four weeks. Active inventory remained below last year's level, and the share of listings with price reductions had declined. But inventory was also beginning to increase compared with the preceding four weeks. That doesn't establish a market shift. Recent pending activity has been relatively steady, and price-cut share continues to ease. Still, the inventory increase is worth monitoring. If inventory continues building while pending activity remains weak, sellers could face greater competition even before the year-over-year inventory comparison turns positive. Try it yourself: Switch the chart above between 6M and YoY. The six-month view shows how inventory has been building recently, while the year-over-year comparison reveals that inventory remains below last year's levels. Both are true, but each tells you something different about the market. The takeaway: A favorable market statistic doesn't mean conditions are standing still. Track recent changes alongside year-over-year trends, and revisit pricing or buying strategies when the evidence begins to shift. items.title: Mortgage Rates Climb in October Amid Accelerating Inflation
items.description: Mortgage Rates Climb in October Amid Accelerating Inflation November 3, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Mortgage rates rose sharply again in October as the U.S. treasury yields surged. According to Freddie Mac , the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.33% in October, up 47 basis points (bps) from September. The rate reached 7.40% in early October, its highest level since 2023, before easing toward the end of the month. Since the conflict in the Middle East began, the 30-year mortgage rate has increased by approximately 128 bps. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.66% in October, up 46 bps from September and 123 bps from the end of February. Compared with a year ago, the average 30-year and 15-year mortgage rates were higher by 108 bps and 117 bps, respectively. The 10-year Treasury yield, a key benchmark for long-term borrowing, increased 21 bps to an average of 5.15% in October, although yields eased during the latter part of the month. Inflation concerns continued to put upward pressure on Treasury yields, as elevated energy prices stemming from the ongoing conflict with Iran contributed to accelerating inflation. Inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August. Energy prices were a major contributor, with fuel oil prices rising 15.3% and gasoline prices increasing 9.1% over the month. At its latest meeting, the Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00%. However, there were two dissenters who voted for a 25 bps increase. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) described economic activity as expanding at a “strong pace,” an improvement from the “solid pace” noted in September. The committee pointed to resilient consumer spending and strong business investment as signs of continued economic strength, while noting that inflation remained elevated and uncertainty persisted. items.title: Retirees, not refis: FOA's 24% growth maps the next market
items.description: Retirees, not refis: FOA's 24% growth maps the next market By Colin McNamara Published November 04, 2026, 3:58 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "Higher rates affect borrower proceeds, but they do not eliminate our customers' need for financial flexibility in retirement." — Kristen Sieffert, President, Finance of America Supporting Data: Finance of America increased its funded volume by 24% year over year in the third quarter. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Reverse mortgage lender Finance of America continues to see its funded volume increase, signaling demand for home equity solutions remains strong in a high-rate environment . Processing Content Volume totaled $748 million in the third quarter, up 24% year over year and 2% from the second quarter , according to FOA's latest earnings release. Since CEO Graham Fleming and President Kristen Sieffert assumed their roles in 2023, the lender has expanded volumes by 20% on average each year, Fleming said on an earnings call Tuesday. The company's forward outlook points to more originations, even as the rest of the mortgage industry reaches a projected downturn. The Mortgage Bankers Association forecasted the forward market to shrink 5% against FOA's double-digit growth. "The difference is demand," Sieffert said on the call. "Ours is driven by retirement need, not refinancing incentives. Higher rates affect borrower proceeds, but they do not eliminate our customers' need for financial flexibility in retirement." Sieffert credited the lender's success to its broad product suite, which features home equity conversion mortgages, its HomeSafe first lien reverse mortgage and second lien reverse mortgage. All three products posted volume increases of 14%, 15% and 63% year over year. FOA also announced the line of credit version of HomeSafe Second will launch soon. The company plans to expand the suite further next year as it moves from a top reverse mortgage lender to a leader in home equity solutions for retirement as a whole, Sieffert said. "Each of our products serves a different homeowner need, and together, they give us multiple paths to growth even when pricing pressure affects individual products," she said. Multiple other companies have launched home equity products this year to try to capture some of this demand. Rocket Mortgage has updated its offerings over the past few years, and said on an earnings call last week its recapture efforts have benefitted the lender's home equity business . FOA's revenue troubles Despite the increased funded volume, FOA posted negative $58 million in total revenue, its first quarter in the red in nearly two years. The lender's net income also dropped to -$110 million from -$29 million in the second quarter of this year and third quarter of 2025, according to the release. On an adjusted basis, FOA totaled a net income of $6 million, or $0.28 per share, still well below the S&P Capital IQ Pro consensus estimate of $1.26 per share. The lender blamed the poor financial showing on lower revenue margins in its retirement solutions segment, which were impacted by the increase in benchmark rates during the quarter. "We consider these as temporary in nature, not because we anticipate the rate environment to move in our favour, but because of the nature of our platform," Matt Engel, chief financial officer, said on the call. items.title: Houston Retail Market Strengthens
items.description: Houston Retail Market Strengthens Houston's retail market maintained healthy fundamentals during Q3 2026, supported by stable occupancy, continued rental growth, and positive tenant demand. Lee & Associates reports that direct vacancy remained at 5.6% for the second consecutive quarter, while the average direct asking NNN rent increased to a record $22.03 per square foot, approximately 8.1% above Q3 2025. Retail demand strengthened during Q3 2026, with net absorption reaching 551,122 square feet, a significant improvement from 39,756 square feet in the previous quarter. Leasing activity totaled approximately 1.75 million square feet, bringing year-to-date leasing activity to nearly 5.9 million square feet. Through the first nine months of 2026, Houston recorded more than 1.1 million square feet of positive net absorption. Development activity emerged as one of the quarter's most notable trends. Houston's construction pipeline expanded to approximately 5.1 million square feet, the highest level since 2019, while quarterly deliveries moderated to approximately 449,000 square feet. items.title: Donalds Makes History With Win For Florida Governor, Voters OK Property Tax Amendment
items.description: Florida voters showed up — even as some poll locations were moved due to severe flooding — to elect Byron Donalds as the state’s 47th governor, succeeding Gov. Ron Desantis . Donalds makes history as the Sunshine State's first Black governor. In addition to electing the state’s first new governor in seven years, voters passed a property tax amendment that increases homestead exemptions significantly over the next two years. Bisnow/Chloe Gallivan Donalds won with 50.1% of the vote, a 1.4-percentage-point lead over his opponent, Democrat David Jolly . “As your next governor, we are going to make sure that Florida remains the very best state in all of America,” Donalds said at his watch party at Broward County’s Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Hollywood. “We're going to be focused on the issues that I've been talking about on this campaign trail for a long time. We are going to drive down costs for the people of this state.” Both candidates and their campaigns leaned heavily on their approaches to affordability, a leading issue for Florida, which is experiencing an outflow of middle-class residents citing affordability concerns. The trend is especially evident in South Florida, where an affordable housing crisis is brewing amid an influx of wealthy individuals. Miami-Dade County lost more than 10,000 residents between 2024 and 2025, placing it among the three counties with the nation’s largest population declines, according to the Census Bureau . Donalds, who has spent the last 10 years in Florida politics and serves as the U.S. representative for Florida’s 19th Congressional District, wants to lower homebuilding costs to boost housing inventory. He has called for smaller units from developers, removing zoning restraints, specifically in Miami-Dade County, and promoted the removal of local zoning restraints to boost housing inventory. The new governor-elect, a Florida State University graduate, also supports the state seeking technology to modernize permitting systems. In addition to a focus on affordability, Donalds pushed to expand transparency on healthcare costs and government spending, worked to move NASA’s headquarters and the Space Force Academy to Florida, and focused on early literacy for children. Jolly, a lawyer and former Republican congressman who turned Democrat in 2025, launched his run in June 2025, campaigning on affordability largely through property insurance, calling for state-backed funding to cover hurricane and wind risk with aims to cut premiums by up to 70%. He also supported using state money to invest in workforce and affordable housing and expanding down payment assistance. “The movement we started doesn't go away tomorrow,” Jolly said onstage at the Tampa Convention Center, where he held his watch party. “It exists to hold our leaders accountable.” Donalds’ win keeps Florida’s 28-year red streak alive, even after high expectations for Jolly’s performance, and falls in line with the real estate industry’s preferences . Wikimedia Commons/Gage Skidmore Byron Donalds at AmericaFest 2025 Some of South Florida’s largest commercial real estate investors funneled millions into Donalds’ campaign in recent months. It had amassed more than $150M by Tuesday, according to the Florida Department of State’s campaign finance database . That is a massive lead against the roughly $14M Jolly collected in donations by Election Day. Among the largest donors to Donalds were Citadel founder Ken Griffin , who donated $15M in two separate payments in July and August, and Related Ross head Stephen Ross , who donated $1M, according to the database. Other donors included Related Group , JDS Development ’s Michael Stern , Oak Row Equities and Property Markets Group . Jolly’s campaign landed donations from Compass agent Michelle Howland and Deborah Simon, daughter of Simon Property Group co-founder Melvin Simon. Florida’s new governor will be sworn into office in January. On top of heavy real estate backing, Donalds earned an almost immediate endorsement from President Donald Trump when he announced he was running for governor in February 2025 and later landed DeSantis’ backing . Beyond electing a new governor, voters approved a property tax amendment targeting housing costs, clearing the 60% hurdle to pass. The amendment will raise Florida’s $50K homestead exemption to $150K next year and $250K in 2028 without exempting tax levies for school district properties. Despite touting greater affordability for homeowners, localities have warned that the amendment’s passage could mean multimillion-dollar cuts to their budgets. In response to the measure, the city of Miami prepared a 25% budget cut to local hospitals, police, fire, parks, public schools and water management, which Related Group's Jorge Peréz cautioned could stunt the city’s ability to attract and retain residents. Landlords may carry the weight if municipalities opt to raise taxes on commercial properties to fund the gap. Rental properties that aren’t homesteaded, because they aren’t owner-occupied, could see a rise in property taxes, which could be passed on to renters . “Anytime some commercial businesses get their costs raised, they tend to pass it on to the consumer,” Kaufman Rossin tax principal and leader Ken Rios said. “So talking about affordability for the rental market, if the commercial owners are paying more, they may increase rents and it may impact the consumer.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Byron Donalds , David Jolly , Ron DeSantis

items.title: Cotality: Northeast, Midwest drive US home-price growth in September
items.description: Cotality: Northeast, Midwest drive US home-price growth in September by John Yellig November 04, 2026 National home-price growth rose 1.7% year over year in September but dipped 0.3% compared to August, with the annual increase being driven by strong results in the Northeastern and Great Lakes states that offset weakness in the West and South, Cotality said in its monthly Home Price Insights report . Compared with August, appreciation strengthened in about half of U.S. metros and weakened in the other half, suggesting no single national trajectory, Cotality said. Illinois led the nation in price growth with a 6.9% increase. The month-over-month dip to $429,500 was the largest decline since 2022 and the third September in a row without monthly growth, Cotality noted, blaming the softness on high mortgage rates that cooled summer demand. Normally, home prices rise 0.2% from August to September. “Potential homebuyers are feeling the pinch from rising costs across the board, especially for daily living expenses,” Cotality Chief Economist Selma Hepp said. “Meanwhile, limited job opportunities and slow wage growth are making households reluctant to move.” Looking ahead, Cotality expects home-price growth of just 0.9% for the 12 months through September. “Elevated mortgage rates are expected to limit home-buying opportunities in 2027,” Hepp said. “However, more inventory and greater buyer bargaining power will keep home-price growth subdued, improving affordability. items.title: UDR beats Q3 estimates and raises guidance, after Apollo deal
items.description: UDR beats Q3 estimates and raises guidance, after Apollo deal The REIT’s executives saw rents increasing, retention hitting record highs and San Francisco thriving at the end of Q3 as they continue making stock buybacks. Published Nov. 3, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Almost two weeks after its massive $2 billion joint venture with Apollo, UDR reported third-quarter results with adjusted funds from operations of $0.65, beating analysts' estimates. In the process, the Highlands Ranch, Colorado-based REIT, which released preliminary Q3 results with the Apollo announcement, raised its same-store net operating income guidance by 37.5 basis points at the midpoint, lowered expense guidance by 35 basis points at the midpoint to 2.9% and raised adjusted FFO guidance by $0.02 at the midpoint to $2.55, according to its earnings release. On the Nov. 3 Q3 earnings call, UDR Chief Operating Officer Mike Lacy said the REIT’s same-store revenue growth of 1.8% was driven by 2% blended lease rate growth. It posted a delinquency rate of around 60 basis points, down 50 basis points year over year. “Third-quarter results reflected better late-quarter leasing trends as compared to recent years,” Lacy said. UDR’s resident retention of 52% represented a Q3 record and was 370 basis points higher than a year earlier, according to Lacy. “Fewer move-outs supported blended lease growth and occupancy, and kept same-store expense growth in check at only 2.2%,” he said. With supply falling off, UDR’s management team appears optimistic about a Sun Belt recovery, although coastal markets still produced the strongest revenue growth in Q3. As it sees signs of future rent growth, the REIT continues to expand JV partnerships, sell properties and buy back shares. Market report Not surprisingly, red-hot San Francisco led the way for UDR in Q3, posting 9% YOY revenue growth, according to a filing with the Securities And Exchange Commission. The market produced blended lease rate growth of approximately 13% and occupancy above 97%, according to Lacy. Additionally, he said rent-to-income ratios remain in the low-20% range, which gives the firm room to push rents. New York City also had a strong Q3 with 5.1% YOY revenue growth, followed by Philadelphia, at 3.5%; Baltimore, at 3.1%; and Orange County, California, at 3%. “New York and Philadelphia continue to lead the East Coast, with weighted average same-store revenue growth of approximately 5%, driven by blended lease rate growth of 4.5% and occupancy above 97%,” Lacy said. On the opposite end of the spectrum, supply-heavy Austin, Texas, saw revenue decline by 3.4% YOY , according to the SEC filing. However, there were signs of improvement for the REIT in Texas. “Dallas remained our strongest Sun Belt market, exhibiting positive revenue growth during the quarter,” Lacy said. “Despite continued new lease rate growth weakness, Austin showed strong positive momentum, and was our only Sun Belt market to deliver positive year-over-year NOI growth.” Los Angeles posted UDR’s second-weakest revenue growth market with a 1.5% decline, according to the SEC filing. items.title: Phoenix among top metros for new apartment construction in 2026
items.description: Phoenix among top metros for new apartment construction in 2026 by Emily Marek November 04, 2026 Across the U.S., apartment construction declined 27% from 2025. The Phoenix metropolitan area will add 17,293 new apartment units this year. The only metros adding more units are New York and Dallas-Fort Worth, according to a new report from RentCafe . Specifically, a majority of those units — 6,013 — are located in Phoenix proper, making it the No. 7 city in the United States for new apartment construction. Gilbert and Mesa followed at 1,647 units and 1,612, respectively. Glendale, Maricopa, Tempe and Avondale will also see just over 1,000 new units each. Across the U.S., apartment construction declined 27% from 2025: The country saw 605,768 new units last year and will see approximately 442,395 this year. Apartment deliveries previously peaked in 2024 at 664,599 units. 2026’s volume will likely fall more in line with 2021 levels, when almost 452,000 units joined the market. Regionally, the South will account for nearly half of all new units in 2026, with Texas and Florida leading the charge. The West will follow, accounting for 23% of new apartments. California, Arizona and Washington will contribute the most units in the region. The Northeast will account for 18% of all new units in 2026, surpassing year-ago production by nearly 80,000 apartments. It will be the only region in the U.S. where apartment deliveries exceed 2025 volumes. Finally, the Midwest will add just 12% of the country’s new units in 2026. items.title: Mortgage Applications Decline as Higher Rates Boost ARM Share
items.description: Mortgage Applications Decline as Higher Rates Boost ARM Share November 4, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Mortgage application activity declined in October as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose sharply again . The Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) Market Composite Index, a measure of total mortgage application volume, fell 14.1% month-over-month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. Compared to a year ago, total mortgage applications were 39.8% lower. Higher fixed mortgage rates continued to drive borrowers toward adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs), whose share of total applications increased to 10.8%. Steep declines occurred in both major components as the average contract rate for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage jumped 35 basis points (bps) to an average of 7.4% in October. Purchase applications decreased 11.9% from September, while refinance applications declined 17.3%. Relative to October 2025, purchase and refinance activity were also down 17.3% and 58.5%, respectively. Meanwhile, the average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs was 6.4% in October. The lower initial interest rate and monthly payments made ARMs relatively more attractive to borrowers, contributing to a 0.7% increase month-over-month. Nonetheless, ARMs remained 31.1% lower than a year ago. The ARMs share of total applications for October increased 1.5 percentage points to 10.8%. Meanwhile, applications for fixed-rate mortgages declined 15.5% month-over-month and 40.7% year-over-year. Average loan sizes declined across most categories in October. The overall loan size decreased 1.5% to $375,200. Purchase loans, however, saw a marginal increase of 0.5% to an average loan size of $448,500. Meanwhile, the average refinance loan size declined 8.0% to $257,840, and ARMs loan size declined 4.8% to an average of $854,180. items.title: Housing Market Feels the Chill as Buyers Pull Back—but Sellers Are Not Panicking Yet
items.description: The national housing market is feeling the chill as high borrowing costs are forcing frustrated buyers to throw in the towel, yet sellers are largely digging in to wait out the slump. Two key metrics— price cuts and delistings —tell the story of American home sellers' resilience in the face of adversity this fall. Across the U.S., about 4.4% of active listings were pulled off the market in October, down from 4.6% a year ago, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly housing market trends report released on Wednesday. On a monthly basis, the delisting rate has ticked up slightly from 4% in September, in line with typical seasonal trends, but no more than that, even with mortgage rates well exceeding 7% and buyer demand waning. According to Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel , delistings matter because they act as a canary in the coal mine. A jump in the delistings rate could be a sign of a housing market in distress. However, the October findings show that sellers are not ready to take their ball and go home yet. "Job relocations, family circumstances, and financial challenges are among the top reasons I am seeing sellers stay on the market rather than withdraw and wait until spring," Josh Stimpson , a real estate agent at The Realtive Group of Reliant Realty in Nashville, TN, tells Realtor.com. "The rising cost of living is also a major factor, prompting many sellers to seek more affordable housing." Price cuts plateau The other key data point used to assess the strength of the U.S. housing market is price cuts. According to the latest housing market data, much like with delistings, there has not been a dramatic change up or down in the share of listings offering discounts, although it remained elevated. For the fourth consecutive month, more than 1 in 5 active listings (20.5%) saw a price cut, marking the highest October reading since 2022 and the second highest this year, trailing only September, which set a four-year record. However, Krimmel points out that the national price cut rate actually retreated 0.3 percentage points month over month, snapping a nine-month streak of monthly gains. Annually, the share of active listings with price cuts ticked up by just 0.2 percentage points. Sellers "are getting used to not everything selling quickly," Learka Bosnak , an agent with of Heather & Learka Team at Douglas Elliman in Beverly Hills, CA , tells Realtor.com. "They aren’t seeing compelling evidence that a slightly lower price will lead to a quick sale. Plus, they aren't feeling a lot of pressure monthly because so many have low-interest-rate mortgages." Loading... A pause, not a panic Taken together, the October delisting and price cut readouts lead to one conclusion concerning the present state of the market. "Right now, it looks more like a seller pause than an exodus," says Krimmel. "Sellers are disengaging rather than showing signs of distress." Regionally, price reductions remained least common in the systemically undersupplied Northeast (16.8% of listings) and most common in the West (21.9%), with the Midwest and South falling in between at 21% each. Across the 50 largest metro markets, 12 saw price cuts on a quarter or more of the listings, unchanged from September. Thirty-four of the metros are running above their year-ago cut rate, down from 36 in September. At the local level, price discounts in October were most common in Indianapolis (31.8%), Denver (31.3%), and Portland, OR (31.1%). While the delisting and price cut numbers stop short of signaling a panic among sellers, October trends do point to a noticeable pullback. New listings and pending sales slump New listings—a measure of homeowners putting their properties on the market—dropped 9.5% from September and 7.5% from a year ago, marking the steepest decline in more than three years. "Sellers know this is a poor time to list, and you do not list into weak demand unless you need to," notes Krimmel. At the same time, pending sales plunged 10.5% year over year—the biggest annual drop since October 2023. However, active listings jumped 7.4% year over year, topping 1.18 million homes for sale—the fourth consecutive month of accelerated growth. This reflects properties piling up on the market as buyers see their purchasing power diminished by surging 30-year mortgage rates, which averaged 7.33% in October. For context, that is a staggering 107 basis points above October 2025 levels and 53 basis points higher than at the start of September. "Elevated interest rates and ongoing affordability challenges have caused many buyers to pause, and the midterm election may be adding to that hesitation," notes Stimpson. "As a result, showing activity has declined and days on market are rising, particularly in Nashville and the surrounding areas." Silver lining for buyers However, patient buyers willing to stick it out can still find attractive deals and see their negotiating position strengthened. "Buyers can often retain their inspection, appraisal, and financing contingencies while also requesting additional repairs, a longer closing period, or a home warranty," says Stimpson. "Properties with extended market exposure may offer even greater leverage, including opportunities to negotiate a lower purchase price or secure seller concessions." Looking ahead to late fall and winter, the Nashville agent says there are some encouraging signs on the horizon, including gradually easing mortgage rates, closings holding steady in Middle Tennessee , and premium listings continuing to attract multiple offers. Yet, both Stimpson and Bosnak agree that what the market sorely lacks is a sense of certainty. "No one is sure what the market or the world will look like in a year, so it doesn’t feel weird to lean into that wait-and-see part of human nature," says the Beverly Hills agent. items.title: JD Vance Blames Iran War for GOP Rout as Mortgage Rates Soared
items.description: Vice President JD Vance is blaming Republicans' election losses on the Iran conflict and rising prices. "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance said in a post on X, hours after Democrats shellacked Republicans in the midterm elections , flipping almost three dozen seats in the House and Senate to win control of both chambers. Vance noted that polling found the war in Iran and cost of living and inflation concerns were the top items on voters' minds heading into Election Day. Those were among the top reasons that many of the voters who helped propel President Donald Trump to a second term in 2024, with majorities in both chambers of Congress, voted in Democrats on Tuesday, Vance said. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance said in the post. "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance said. Indeed, Americans were broadly concerned about affordability in the months leading up to the election. While Trump said he remained focused on it, he spent the run-up to the election detailing projects in Washington, DC, such as a botched effort to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool . Both Democrats and Republicans have promised their own affordability agendas for the coming months. But in swing states that turned against Trump , including Iowa , Ohio , Texas , and Maine , housing affordability was at the top of voters' minds. So, too, have many young voters worried that homeownership is rising out of reach . Inflation worries Most markers of inflation show many costs have risen sharply this year. Gas prices often embody Americans' concerns, and AAA reports the national average price for gas is $4.12 a gallon, compared to $3.05 a year ago. Trump, for his part, continued defending his economic record on Tuesday, telling media outlets that night that he would accept the election results and might seek common ground with Democrats. But then he also posted an image of a red hat with the word "veto" on it, before celebrating the rise of the Dow the next morning following the results. "Stock Market just hit another Record High—91 Days in just a short period of time—Less than two years," he posted to Truth Social on Wednesday. "Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!" And yet, the war in Iran and its resultant rise in oil prices and other costs hamstrung efforts to improve affordability. The Federal Reserve hiked interest rates earlier this year, and kept them steady in its most recent meeting. Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee in recent months show that leaders are worried that inflation is stickier than expected and that the conflict with Iran will continue to drive up costs. Vance said in his post that it was "sound" political advice to call for a diplomatic solution to the Iran conflict. He also indicated that he could be open for change to the controversial immigration enforcement policies that have deeply affected the housing market and home construction. "I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance," Vance said in the post. "But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you." Democrats take aim at affordability Meanwhile, Democratic leaders said in a press conference on Wednesday that they would focus on affordability in the coming term. Loading... "We're going to fight hard for the heartland of America," New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to become the new Speaker of the House, said on Wednesday. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries , who is likely to become the new Speaker of the House, repeatedly avoided discussing Trump. Instead, he said his focus was on "affordability and accountability." "We know we have to undertake, with the seriousness of purpose, a relentless effort to make life more affordable for everyday Americans," Jeffries said. Later he added, "We have been focused, relentlessly, on dealing with the affordability crisis and driving down the high cost of living." Massachusetts Rep. Katherine Clark , who is currently minority whip but stands as a contender to become House majority leader, said that could include efforts to roll back the president's tariffs , which have driven up the cost of many homebuilding materials and household goods . Jeffries said the House Democratic Caucus will convene next week and lay out a clear plan for what to do next. But neither he nor Sen. Chuck Schumer had heard directly from Trump on Wednesday. NAR calls for bipartisanship The National Association of Realtors®, in a Wednesday statement, called for more progress on housing. “Regardless of which party controls Congress, NAR’s priorities remain the same: increasing housing supply, improving affordability, protecting property rights and expanding access to homeownership," NAR said. "Our research shows that 85% of Americans believe homeownership is part of the American Dream, underscoring why housing must remain a priority for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle." RPAC-supported candidates won in at least 325 races, and a number of ballot initiatives this year involved housing-related issues . NAR also noted the bipartisanship of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act , the housing package aimed at making it easier to build homes. Congress passed it this summer with large majorities from both parties. "We will continue building on that momentum, working with REALTOR® champions and real estate allies in both parties to advance commonsense solutions that bring more homes to the market and help more Americans achieve the dream of homeownership," NAR said. items.title: Laundry Room Locations in New Homes and Apartments, 2025
items.description: Laundry Room Locations in New Homes and Apartments, 2025 November 4, 2026 Onnah Dereski No Comments In 2025, the majority of homes started featured laundry connections on the first floor (70%), according to the Census’s Survey of Construction . Laundry located on the second floor or higher was the second most prevalent at 27%. The basement, garage, and other locations all had a 1% or lower share. In NAHB’s What Home Buyer’s Really Want , home buyers are surveyed on where they would like their laundry located. While the first floor remained the most desired location for laundry at 58%, preferences diverged significantly for other locations. The basement was the second most popular choice at 19%, followed by the garage at 16%, and only 7% for the second floor or higher. This comparison highlights a possible disconnect between what builders are offering and what buyers are seeking. While builders are largely opting for laundry connections on the first or second floor, a notable portion of buyers prefer the basement or garage. This variance is shown in the chart below. Across all Census Divisions, the first floor remains the most common location for laundry. Nevertheless, some regional differences exist. In the West South Central division, 93% of homes had a laundry area on the first floor, compared to just 49% in the New England. Meanwhile, a second-floor laundry was most popular in New England at 41%, and least common in the West South Central at 6%. Not surprisingly, laundry connections in basements are more common in areas of the country where basements themselves are more common: primarily in the northern regions. The West North Central division led with 13% of homes featuring a basement laundry, followed by New England at 9%. Among age-restricted homes, where accessibility and main-level living are key design priorities, 89% featured laundry on the first floor. Multifamily Laundry Trends For multifamily units completed 1 in 2025, 87% of apartments included an individual laundry, while 13% offered shared or no laundry facilities. This share has remained relatively stable since 2015, reflecting continued renter demand for in-unit laundry. Regionally, the Northeast has the highest shared or no laundry facilities percentage at 37%. In contrast, shared or no laundry facilities remained far less common elsewhere: 16% in the West, 10% in the Midwest, and 4% in the South. items.title: LGI Homes Q3 2026 earnings reveal leadership test in downturn
items.description: A peculiar phenomenon in homebuilding has fascinated me for much of the past two-plus decades. In virtually every market, across almost every customer segment and price point, a handful of homebuilders consistently outperform competitors facing essentially the same business conditions. They face the same mortgage rates, land and development costs, labor constraints, household purchasing-power challenges and regulatory obstacles. They work with essentially the same raw materials, including people, capital, building products, subcontractors and operating processes. Yet their results can differ dramatically, especially when business conditions turn difficult. A decade or so ago, a highly regarded homebuilding business strategist mused aloud to me about this phenomenon. He was struck by how companies dealt with essentially the same competitive hand, yet a few outlier leaders figured out how to produce better results than the rest. I've thought about that observation often, particularly during periods when the industry's cyclical pressures expose the difference between companies that can withstand adversity and those that can turn adversity into an opportunity to strengthen their businesses. The distinction is especially relevant now. U.S. homebuilders are facing an unforgiving mix of weak selling conditions, elevated capital costs, stubbornly high land and development expenses, and households whose purchasing power has failed to keep pace with the cost of homeownership. These pressures have persisted long enough to strain business plans based on more favorable assumptions, and little is certain about when conditions will improve. Which brings us to LGI Homes , its Q3 2026 earnings report, and a question that extends well beyond a single company's quarterly performance: What distinguishes homebuilding enterprises whose leaders and organizations can emerge from a prolonged downturn stronger than they entered it? LGI's third quarter: A revealing contradiction LGI Homes' November 3 earnings report is a useful case study because its operating results show both encouraging evidence of management's execution and unmistakable signs that the business faces tough sledding ahead. The Woodlands, Texas-based builder reported 1,222 home closings in the third quarter, including 33 currently or previously leased homes, a 10.4% increase from the year-earlier quarter. Homebuilding revenues rose 10.3% to $437.5 million, and net income increased to $24.6 million, or $1.05 per diluted share, compared with $19.7 million, or $0.85 per share, in the year-earlier quarter. Profitability and expense management emerged as clear strengths. Homebuilding gross margin reached 20.2%, and adjusted homebuilding gross margin was 23.7%, both up 40 basis points sequentially. Selling, general and administrative expenses declined 2.5% in absolute dollars, while SG&A as a percentage of total revenue improved 180 basis points year over year, reflecting operational rigor and executional excellence. The company also reduced its net debt-to-capital ratio to 40.6%, up 420 basis points from a year earlier, and ended September with $447.7 million in liquidity. Its active community count increased by 7.1% year over year to 151. Yet a forward-looking lens tells a far less rosy story. Net orders plunged 61.2% to 609 homes, down from 1,570 a year earlier, while the cancellation rate rose to 53.8% from 33.6%. Backlog declined 47.5% to 685 homes. Management narrowed its full-year closing guidance to 4,600 to 4,800 homes, reflecting weaker sales activity and ongoing affordability pressures. These results speak of the vulnerability of LGI's business model at a time when the company's core customer is among the most financially constrained in the housing market. LGI has built much of its business around helping renters become homeowners through a direct-to-consumer sales model, speculative construction, and a value proposition that emphasizes attainable monthly payments. These capabilities have helped distinguish the company for years. They also leave its sales performance especially vulnerable to turbulent headwinds, such as mortgage-rate movements and changes in buyer qualification. The third-quarter numbers make it clear that LGI's operational strengths have not shielded it from those pressures. Will the capabilities that helped the company develop its distinctive business model now enable it to adapt more effectively than competitors under the same conditions? Wall Street sees the strengths and the vulnerabilities Wolfe Research's November 3 assessment of LGI serves as an important counterweight to any temptation to interpret the company's earnings performance as evidence that it has already mastered the current downturn. Analyst Trevor Allinson and his team credited LGI's Q3 operating performance, namely its gross-margin strength and SG&A expense reductions, while maintaining a Peer Perform rating. Wolfe noted that LGI's predominantly self-developed land position supports margins at a time when several competitors have sustained hits to sequential margins. Wolf Research's analysis also explicitly recognizes LGI's process-driven organization as a competitive strength, citing the company's ability to pare back operating errors in land acquisition, construction efficiency and warranty management. This is not to say that Wall Street exactly overlooks the value of management execution or organizational capability. Wolfe's analysis shows that analysts recognize those strengths and attempt to account for their financial impact. items.title: Finance of America grows origination volume but reports $110M loss in Q3
items.description: Finance of America ( FOA ) reported a net loss of $110 million in the third quarter of 2026, as noncash fair value adjustments weighed on results despite growth in the company's home equity lending business. The Plano, Texas-based company on Tuesday reported $748 million in funded volume for the quarter ending Sept. 30, up 24% from $603 million during the same period last year. Year-to-date funded volume reached $2.07 billion, a 17% increase from the first nine months of 2025. FOA recorded a basic loss of $5.24 per share, compared with a loss of 98 cents per share in the third quarter of 2025. The quarterly net loss was primarily driven by $125 million in noncash fair value adjustments. On an adjusted basis, FOA reported net income of $6 million, or 28 cents per share, compared with $33 million, or $1.33 per share, a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA totaled $17 million, down from $55 million in the third quarter of 2025. “The third quarter of 2026 demonstrated the continued strength of our platform, with funded origination volume growing 24% year over year. While higher interest rates drove near-term pressure on earnings , we believe this impact is temporary,” CEO Graham Fleming said in a statement. “We have already taken steps to improve margins.” During the company's earnings call, Fleming said the company remains focused on production growth, operational efficiency and cash generation, and explained that margins compressed after the Federal Reserve shifted from cutting to raising interest rates. "We have already made the necessary changes to product pricing, and we expect margins to return to historical levels in the first half of 2027," Fleming told investors. "Finance of America has grown volumes on average by 20% each year since 2023. The third quarter was a challenging rate environment, with the 10-year Treasury yields increasing over 75 basis points during the quarter, a reaction to the Fed's pivot to raising rates and elevated inflation," he added. Retirement solutions performance FOA’s retirement solutions segment, which originates home equity-based financing products, including reverse mortgages , recorded $748 million in funded volume during the quarter, up 24% year over year. "Our retirement solutions revenue margin was impacted in the third quarter, decreasing to 9%, compared with 11.3% in the third quarter of 2025, and a historical average since the start of 2024 of 10.7%," Fleming said during the call. "We believe these impacts are temporary and do not change the underlying fundamentals of our business." Revenue for the segment totaled $67 million, down 1% from the prior-year period and a decrease from Q2 2026 's $74 million. Pretax income fell to $3 million, down from $10 million a year earlier, while adjusted net income declined to $9 million, down from $20 million. The company attributed the decline in profitability primarily to pressure on origination margins as benchmark interest rates increased during the quarter. It said it implemented product and pricing adjustments to address the impact and expects margins to return to historical levels. For the first nine months of 2026, the retirement solutions segment generated $2.07 billion in funded volume, up 17% year over year. Revenue increased 14% to $208 million. "Since 2023, our submission volumes have increased by 21% annually, while our funded volume has grown by 20% annually. This is across our product suite, as HECM volume is up 14% year over year, HomeSafe first liens are up 15%, and HomeSafe seconds are up 63%," FOA President Kristen Sieffert said during the call. Portfolio management performance FOA's portfolio management segment, which generates revenue through net interest income and fair value changes on portfolio assets, reported a pretax loss of $138 million, compared with an $11 million loss in the third quarter of 2025. The company attributed the loss primarily to negative non-cash fair value adjustments on retained interests in securitizations. Portfolio management reported adjusted net income of $11 million, down from $30 million a year earlier. Assets under management in the segment increased 23% year over year to $37.4 billion. The growth reflected new originations and the acquisition of Onity Mortgage Corp. ‘s HECM servicing portfolio on July 1. For the first nine months of 2026, portfolio management recorded a pretax loss of $128 million, compared with pretax income of $202 million in the same period last year. Adjusted net income totaled $57 million, down from $66 million. FOA ended the third quarter with $118 million in cash and cash equivalents, up from $85 million at the end of June. The company attributed the increase to cash generation from originations and capital markets activity. Total equity stood at $307 million as of Sept. 30, including $259 million attributable to common stock. Book value was $28.08 per common share. The company said it expects to complete a $60 million paydown of senior secured notes in November. Looking ahead to the final quarter of 2026, chief financial officer Matt Engel said the company expects funded volume to reach $3.1 billion to $3.4 billion, a range "supported by consumer demographics , our product breadth, and ongoing conversion improvements." items.title: MSRs trade at richest levels in decades as lenders, funds pile in
items.description: Chicago-based Rate has recently changed its servicing strategy, retaining mortgage servicing rights ( MSRs ) instead of selling. “We've been retaining all of our MSRs for the last 12 months, so we're over $50 billion in MSR retention,” CEO Victor Ciardelli said in an exclusive interview with HousingWire . “We really believe in retaining the MSRs, staying close to the customer.” Rate’s approach reflects a broader trend of mortgage lenders holding onto their portfolios or seeking to add MSRs as a way to recapture borrowers when rates eventually fall. John Sullivan, managing director of MSR advisory services at Milliman , has seen that shift firsthand. Speaking during IMN’s Mortgage Servicing Rights Conference in New York on Monday, he said he’s having more conversations with clients about retaining their portfolios “unless liquidity is an issue,” and about monetizing them if they are not hedging . Higher demand for MSRs is not limited to independent mortgage banks ( IMBs ). Depository institutions are also showing more interest, executives told HousingWire during the conference. “ Banks historically are not great at recapture, but we think that given some changes on the Basel capital front, we're going to see more bank participation in this space on a go-forward basis, and I think banks will think about just customer acquisition in general, cross-selling in general,” said Larry Goldstone, president of capital markets and lending at BSI Financial Services . Strategic investors are also willing to grow their portfolios. Rob Williams, co-founder and CEO at Grander Investment Management , a specialized asset manager focused on MSRs, said he’s tactical but sees MSRs as a “spectacular asset” that can reach double-digit returns. “I can probably be more patient,” he said during the conference, when comparing his approach to the other buyers. “I can be more tactical.” The buyer base views MSRs through different lenses. Rich McRedmond, managing director at CrossCountry Mortgage , said that while banks see MSRs as part of their consumer banking strategy, real estate investment trusts ( REITs ) see them as a pure investment. And mortgage companies see them as a borrower recapture tool “from when they get the mortgage to when they get the next mortgage.” Multiples and yields Conventional, pristine MSRs are seeing 7x multiples amid high demand, a level not reached in more than two decades. “We've seen some pretty extraordinary multiples of late,” Goldstone said. “This is usually an inexpensive asset, and therefore an asset that people want to be able to own. I think you could hedge MSR pretty effectively and still get low-double digits, high-single digit returns up until about the last year. That's pretty attractive for an asset that really doesn't have a whole lot of credit risk associated with it.” Simon Aldrich, senior executive vice president at Freedom Mortgage , believes that at this point, “it’s very difficult to be in this market if you don’t have recapture.” “In our model, we don't hedge, so I'm not worried about rates going up or rates going down. Rates go up, I get the pickup at slower speeds. Rates go down, our call center kicks into gear.” Bayview Asset Management , which acquires MSRs from the bulk and flow markets and uses five different subservicers, has also built out a full recapture strategy, including through its acquisition of Guild Mortgage . Managing director Michael Lau said Bayview has partnered with investors, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, that have long-duration strategies. “MSRs are great because they're not correlated to the equity or the bond market , and gives them something alternative that also, because we hedge out all the interest rate risk for them, delivers a very consistent return on their money, net of our fees,” Lau said. Opportunistic sales Some companies have taken advantage of current pricing to sell MSRs for different reasons, including to pay back debt or raise funds. In the third quarter , Rocket Companies sold $23 billion of unpaid principal balance (UPB) for $379 million in cash proceeds, retaining the subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the MSRs sold. Analysts told HousingWire the company usually sells production in the wholesale channel due to lower recapture possibility. Pennymac Financial Services entered into an agreement to sell $29 billion in UPB of low-coupon conventional MSRs, with $490 million of proceeds expected to pay down debt. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) sold about $60 billion — at a roughly 6x multiple — to JPMorgan Chase , sources told HousingWire. The companies declined to comment. This is part of a plan to bring up to $80 billion of MSRs to market in the fourth quarter, with the expectation of being paid more than $1.8 billion in an attempt to reduce leverage. Newrez President Baron Silverstein said his company is taking a disciplined approach. Across the Newrez portfolio, 60% of loans were originated before or during the COVID-19 pandemic. “In today's market, given where we are from a rate perspective, there's pressure in a competitive environment where MSRs get created — where that gain on sale is from an all-in gain-on-sale perspective on loans that we originate or buy. And when we think about that, we get very selective and stay very disciplined about how we put that capital to work,” Silverstein said. “When you think about hedging in a market like this, that also requires a lot of capital, and it's very challenging in these markets today, regardless of the interest rate environment. This has been the case for the last year to year and a half.” What's next? items.title: How midterm outcome may shape housing bill follow-up, GSE reform
items.description: How midterm outcome may shape housing bill follow-up, GSE reform By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published November 04, 2026, 1:32 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "I don't see them in the '27-28 years coming out of conservatorship," — Jennifer McGuiness-Lubbert, CEO, Pivot Financial What's at Stake: How much federal money and regulation gets directed toward initiatives that could save borrowers money or require more spending on servicing compliance. With a "blue wave" in Congress and lame-duck lawmakers headed toward a budget deadline, housing bill appropriations Democrats have favored will likely be one near-term mortgage-related priority, one speaker at an industry conference said Tuesday. "It is urgent that 'Road" be funded," Sam Valverde, a former housing official who is now managing director at Falcon Capital Advisors, told attendees at the IMN Mortgage Servicing Rights conference on Tuesday, referring to the 21st Century Road to Housing bill. Processing Content Housing executive orders from the Republican administration may slow, he speculated. "I think you'd want to see what the reset is within the White House around dealing with a new Congress," Valverde said. The administration has made some moves to distance itself from housing issues even before the midterms, with Trump letting the authorization of the housing bill pass but calling it a lower priority and not explicitly backing it. Donald Trump Jr.'s business partner Omeed Malik left Fannie Mae's board just before the election, according to a Securities and Exchange Commission filing. The midterms also could shape how housing agencies, which Democrats have called for more scrutiny of, approach existing EO directives. GSE implications For one, the latest EO calls for the Federal Housing Finance Agency to consider reducing government-sponsored enterprises' loan-level price adjustments for title-waiver-eligible loans, potentially helping lenders but resulting in prepayments investors could view as a risk. "If MSR investors and MBS investors start to understand that policy changes will create repayment activity they cannot anticipate, they're going to ask for an uncertainty premium," Valverde said, noting that the FHFA has discretion on whether to follow through with this. Broader GSE reform, including the possibility of a stock sale, also is something the mortgage industry and investors will be watching closely now because many analysts have indicated that they anticipated it to be on hold until after the midterms. Democrats have generally been less eager to remove the GSEs from conservatorship administratively than Republicans but have been involved in some past legal proposals for reform. Some speakers at the IMN event said that they were skeptical of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's recent statements about a stock sale potentially being on the roadmap for 2027 or 2028, when there is an extendable deadline for conservatorship ending. "Even he is questioning whether the shareholder restructuring is going to help homeowners if mortgage spreads widen in doing so," said Tim Roy, vice president, housing finance policy, at the Independent Community Bankers of America. Jennifer McGuiness-Lubbert, CEO of Pivot Financial, said because plans regarding whether or not to make a share offering or depart conservatorship have changed multiple times, she's skeptical of action. "Even if they were to sell a component of the holdings of the Treasury and take in additional investment dollars. I don't see them in the '27-28 years coming out of conservatorship," she said. Bose George, managing director of Keefe, Bruyette & Woods, said KBW has put 30% odds on the GSEs leaving conservatorship and the percentage could be lower. Capital deficiencies and senior preferred shares remain hurdles, and even though a stock offering does not require Congress, the election sweep "could just make things harder, where other parts of the agenda get tougher to push through," George said. Another federal impact experts have broadly forecast to emerge from the midterms could be more regulation of artificial intelligence. Watch for more AI rules During separate conference discussions about AI, panelists noted that Fannie Mae updated one of its planned 2027 regulatory directives for what the Trump administration has called "superintelligence" not long before the midterms. With it possible to use AI to handle up to 60% of loss mitigation tasks and some states already requiring disclosures and opt-outs around its use, servicers should be prepared for increased regulation, panelists said. "There's a lot that to unpack there from a regulatory environment that will probably only continue to heat up," said Joshua Bishop, chief operating officer, servicing, at Newrez. "You've got to have a good, strong AI governance process." items.title: GSA Taps Cushman & Wakefield Veteran As Federal Real Estate Head
items.description: The General Services Administration has turned to a brokerage veteran to take charge of the government's real estate portfolio after significant turnover at the position. Bisnow/Emily Wishingrad The General Services Administration's National Capital Region Building at 301 Seventh St. SW The GSA appointed Mark Weiss , formerly an executive vice chairman at Cushman & Wakefield, to serve as commissioner of its Public Buildings Service division, the agency announced Wednesday. The PBS commissioner oversees the federal government's nearly 360M SF real estate portfolio. Weiss is the fourth person to fill the role since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025. Two of the previous three PBS commissioners held the role on an interim basis. Michael Peters initially took over the role in January 2025. He oversaw a flurry of GSA activity in his short tenure, with the agency proposing scores of lease terminations and building sales as Trump sought to slash the federal footprint to cut costs. Many of those actions have since been walked back or slowed down. Andrew Heller was named acting PBS commissioner in August 2025, then replaced by Michael Gelber in the role in July. Weiss has more than four decades of commercial real estate experience, working on office leases and advising clients across sectors including finance, law and manufacturing. Based in New York, he has spent the last decade with Cushman & Wakefield and previously worked for the brokerage firms then known as Newmark Knight Frank and Studley, according to his LinkedIn page . Last year, his team brokered a 250K SF lease with Goodwin Procter at 200 Fifth Ave. in Manhattan, which was honored by the Real Estate Board of New York at an awards event in May. “At its core, PBS’s mission is to provide and manage efficient, cost-effective, and mission-ready workplaces that enable federal agencies to serve the American people,” Weiss said in a statement. “We will continue to advance the Trump-Vance Administration’s objectives and maintain the integrity of the federal government’s real estate portfolio.” Also this week, the GSA appointed Jennifer Hill as the commissioner of the Federal Acquisition Service, which oversees the government's procurement and contracting. Hill had been the chief financial officer of Bank of America Merrill Lynch. items.title: U.S. Hotel RevPAR Surges 7% In Q3, But Expect Easing From Here
items.description: Another quarter of strong hotel revenue gains has one executive touting the start of a multiyear upswing for the sector, although that hasn’t resulted in profits for operators, and future growth will likely be more moderate than this year's pace. Pixabay/Rodrigo_SalomonHC U.S. hotels recorded third-quarter increases in occupancy, demand and average daily rate, driving a 7% increase in revenue per available room, according to CBRE’s latest data . Occupancy rose nearly 2% in the quarter, while room demand was up 3% and ADR increased by more than 4%. Pebblebrook Hotel Trust reported an 8.3% year-over-year increase in RevPAR and 7% growth in ADR for Q3. That prompted the luxury hotel REIT to increase its RevPAR outlook by 175 basis points at the midpoint to a range of 5.5% to 6%. “As we look beyond this year, we continue to believe we're at the beginning of a very strong multiyear upcycle for the hotel industry,” Pebblebrook CEO Jon E. Bortz said during the REIT’s earnings call last week. The industry’s other major hotel chains recorded similar RevPAR growth for the quarter. Hyatt Hotels ’ RevPAR was up more than 8% in the U.S., while Marriott International and Hilton were both above 7% growth. IHG Hotels & Resorts and Wyndham Hotels reported RevPAR jumps of 6% or more in the U.S., and Choice Hotels ' increase was a more modest 3.8%. The industry’s rate of growth and the broad recovery in demand were helped by weak comparisons from last year. RevPAR declined in each of the final three quarters of 2025 following President Donald Trump ’s tariff announcements . This year, RevPAR growth has accelerated each quarter, said Jan Freitag , the national director of hospitality analytics for CoStar Group . “Hotel operators were able to raise rates because midweek corporate travel stayed healthy, group demand rebounded, and higher-income leisure travelers kept spending,” Freitag told Bisnow . September was the strongest month of the year, with RevPAR up 11% and occupancy and ADR each up more than 5%. Big events like the World Cup tournament added to the year's momentum, though RevPAR growth was already above 4% before the first match. Plus, the tournament's effect was largely concentrated in July. “The World Cup was a good, strong dose of caffeine in one given month,” said Suraj Bhakta , CEO of hospitality-focused brokerage NewGen Advisory . The industry also benefited from a favorable calendar, with holidays like Independence Day and Yom Kippur falling on weekends. But the growth of weekend and weekday occupancies points to underlying demand beyond those events, Freitag said. Luxury and upper-upscale hotels sold nearly 2 million more group rooms and about 4 million more rooms booked by individual travelers than in the same period of 2025, according to CoStar data. RevPAR in the luxury segment grew more than 9% through August and 13% in September, marking its strongest performance outside the World Cup months since the pandemic rebound. The industry’s limited supply growth, which remains below 1%, also helped drive RevPAR and ADR higher. Bhakta doesn’t expect supply growth to bounce back next year, as construction costs and the cost of capital haven't declined enough to spur new development . The industry’s momentum is expected to help it close out 2026 strong, and analysts forecast it should easily beat the 1% decline in RevPAR recorded in Q4 last year. Forward bookings are slightly ahead of where they were a year ago, suggesting the industry will also outperform CoStar's full-year growth forecast of 4.4%, Freitag said. However, those RevPAR gains didn’t necessarily translate into stronger profits, as rising labor and operating costs cut into revenue gains. During the third quarter, hotel wage growth increased nearly 5% year-over-year, outpacing the national average and the rate of inflation. Hyatt Hotels’ adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was up 1.4% to $295M in Q3, but the company’s revenue fell 2.4% to $1.7B. “Profit gains are concentrated at the high end,” Freitag said. Gross operating profit has risen 7.2% at luxury properties and 4.9% at upper-upscale ones, but it is only up 1.2% through the rest of the sector, according to CoStar. And profit is expected to slow further. CoStar has forecast national gross operating profit per available room growth of 4% in 2026, but just over 1% for next year. After adjusting for inflation, that metric remains roughly 16% below 2019 levels. Bhakta said the hospitality industry could see another solid year in 2027, but it will be hard to show the same kind of RevPAR growth because of the high peak hotels hit this year. “It'll temper a little bit, but it'll still be good,” Bhakta said, predicting 2% to 3% RevPAR growth next year. items.title: U.S. REIT Omega Healthcare Investors Expands Care Home Platform In £615M Deal
items.description: Courtesy of Omega Healthcare Investors Omega Healthcare Investors is pledging to expand its UK care home platform. U.S. healthcare REIT Omega Healthcare Investors and Foundation Partners have acquired UK care home operator Runwood Homes in a £615M deal, adding 55 homes and 3,930 registered beds to their UK platform. The newly acquired homes will be operated by Evera Living, a new care platform established by Foundation Partners, which has partnered with Omega to invest in and grow the business. The companies said they are targeting further acquisitions in the UK care market. Evera Living will be led by John Forrest, formerly chief operating officer of Spire Healthcare, as CEO, with Vishul Seewoolall, previously COO of Signature Care and a regional operations director at Bupa, appointed COO. “Alongside Foundation Partners and Evera’s leadership, we see the opportunity to support a substantial UK care business with the capital and capabilities for its next chapter,” Omega Healthcare Investors Chief Investment Officer Vikas Gupta said in a statement. “The strength of this partnership is evergreen capital that shares our long-term perspective. Together, we want to build a multinational, multi-service care platform. We are thinking in decades, not towards a short-term exit,” Foundation Partners co-founder and Managing Partner Ben Puddle said. Omega, which has a global portfolio of approximately 1,100 care facilities, has been investing in the UK for several years, and its UK portfolio comprised approximately 300 facilities, with the Runwood acquisition taking its UK holdings beyond 350 care homes. Foundation Partners has invested approximately £750M in healthcare over the past decade and acquired and managed six operating platforms, representing more than 70 homes and 3,000 beds before the Runwood deal. Its previous investments include New Century Care, Hartford Care, Graham Care, Select Healthcare and Towerview Care. Runwood was founded by Gordon Sanders 40 years ago and has grown into one of the UK's larger elderly care operators. Knight Frank advised on the sale. items.title: Inside Joe Rogan’s Incredible $14.4 Million Austin Mansion—and Home to His Very Controversial Podcast
items.description: Podcaster Joe Rogan has once again found himself at the center of controversy after he was confronted about his past political views. Rogan, 59, was on the receiving end of scrutiny when comedian Sam Tallent called Rogan out for voting for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election. "Dude it's weird, cuz like, I talk to people a lot who I don't share like, the exact ideals with, like, I don't like that you f—n' endorsed Trump, but like, I have a lot of friends who voted for Trump," Tallent said. Tallent added, "No, it's fine. Listen, it used to be that people used to be able to differ in their opinions and have conversations. But today we have become so divided, and I think a big factor is social media, echo chambers, propaganda, bots, gaslighting. And it seems like there's so much riding on everything constantly, because you're looking at your phone all the time. "And everything on the phone is, 'This is the end. This is the end, this is the beginning of the end, this is a signal of the end, the only hope is to stop this,' and on both sides. People are addicted to their phones, so like, the information you're getting almost all day long is very bleak and very dire." Rogan's podcast has long been known as a hotspot for the internet personality to share his outspoken opinions on everything from from celebrity gossip to political policy. "The Joe Rogan Experience," which he records largely at his $14.4 million home in Austin, TX , is widely regarded as one of the most successful podcasts in the world, but it seems listeners on Apple have a different opinion. The news came shortly before Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko accused the podcaster of "pushing Russian propaganda on his podcast," amid the war in Ukraine. Klitschko slammed Rogan's comments about President Joe Biden 's decision to provide U.S.-made missiles to Ukrainian forces. In a previous episode with music producer Scott Storch , the two discussed their relief that Trump had won the election, and then criticized the Biden administration for providing Ukraine with long-range missiles for use in its war with Russia. “I feel safer knowing that Trump is in office,” Storch told Rogan. “What I don’t feel safer about is that now they’re launching missiles into Russia,” Rogan replied. “How are you allowed to do that when you’re on the way out? [There] should be, like, some sort of, like, a pause for, like, significant actions that could potentially start World War III. “Yeah, [Vladimir] Putin should not have invaded Ukraine, yes, 100%, but don’t start World War III,” Rogan added.
