A great America is not an America that abandons countries that defend freedom with their lives.” Klitschko offered to come on Rogan's podcast so they could further discuss the topic as "free men." Rogan is no stranger to provoking outrage and controversy with his comments, and his show retains the top spot in Spotify's rankings. However, his lackluster showing in the Apple charts will no doubt come as something of a surprise to the podcaster. Indeed, Rogan's show has proven so popular that even Vice President Kamala Harris reportedly considered an appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience." She ultimately opted for the more female-focused "Call Her Daddy" with host Alexandra Cooper . Loading... items.title: Before Your Insurance Deductible Resets, Here's What to Know About Medical Imaging

items.title: UWM holds 115-130bp margins while rivals cut to stay afloat
items.description: UWM holds 115-130bp margins while rivals cut to stay afloat By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 04, 2026, 1:54 p.m. EST | Updated November 04, 2026, 3:36 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: Wholesale lenders struggling to keep up production and invest in artificial intelligence. Forward Look: Brace for UWM to make smaller mortgage servicing rights sales to attract more buyers. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. United Wholesale Mortgage expects to keep fourth-quarter gain on sale margins in its 115-to-130 basis point range, even as some wholesale competitors price down to 70 to 80 basis points to "win loans and stay afloat," Chairman, CEO and President Mat Ishbia said on the company's third quarter earnings call. Ishbia argued that scale is what lets UWM hold pricing where others can't. The company can absorb a $35 million AI investment and "spread it over a lot of loans," he said, adding that "there aren't any other companies that can do it at that level," with only a couple of rivals close enough in size to try. Processing Content The operating gaps at other lenders, he said, come down to volume: "they don't have enough business, they don't have enough opportunity to get loans, they can't keep up production, they can't invest in AI." UWM's own weak spot over the past year was capital, Ishbia acknowledged, and it was fixed by "someone writing a check and with me and Oaktree partnering to do that." The company returned to profitability at $212.5 million, at the midpoint of the range provided on Oct. 23 when it dropped preliminary results in advance of the pricing of its rights offering related to the capital raise. UWM beats estimates Keefe, Bruyette & Woods calculated operating income at 4 cents per share, which beat its outlook by 2 cents per share and consensus by one cent, analyst Bose George said in a flash note prior to the earnings call. "Operating trends were largely in line and the beat came from a combination of lower amortization (1 cent) and lower expenses (1 cent)," George explained. As for its servicing income, the 12% increase over the second quarter to $246.6 million, was in line with KBW's revised $249 million estimate. "Positive MSR valuation marks of $632.9 million were partially offset by $481.5 million of derivative losses, resulting in a net valuation gain of $151.3 million, which drove the higher GAAP income versus operating," George said. Turning around UWM's 2Q loss In the second quarter, UWM Holdings lost $451.9 million , driven by a hedge-related loss due to a position it took in anticipation of acquiring Two Harbors Investment. The initial agreement between the two companies fell apart and UWM would lose a bidding war with CrossCountry. This hedge loss is why UWM needed the Oaktree and Ishbia family funding in the first place. UWM posted a $12.1 million profit in the third quarter of 2025. Origination volume was previously reported at $33.4 billion. This trails Rocket's $43.6 billion , which includes $10.1 billion of correspondent purchases. How UWM's servicing sale is progressing At the same time UWM announced preliminary earnings, it also revealed plans to sell $70 billion to $80 billion of mortgage servicing rights in the current quarter. When asked why the company sold a significant amount of MSRs, Ishbia said he did not see it this way. He pointed to total sales of $135 billion to $140 billion this year and $180 billion in 2025. The amount is less than its total production this year. "I do think it's a great opportunistic thing for UWM," Ishbia said. "I'm big on de-risking, deleveraging; it creates cash, it helps us in a lot of different respects. We're always looking at that opportunity, and we'll look at it again more this quarter or next quarter or whenever the opportunity is there." However, selling large portfolios also means the company has to take a "liquidity discount," and in the future it will look at making smaller sales, which opens the transactions up to more buyers, Ishbia said. 'Rocket means zero' to Ishbia Ishbia was asked about Rocket's statement during its call about adding 200 brokers . "So first off, Rocket means zero to me, they just make numbers up," Ishbia said. "None of that's true, but either way, they can say what they want to say." He added he does not need to talk about what Rocket does, but what he likes about what they and other wholesalers are doing is showing, "the brokers are the place to win." Regarding repaying the Oaktree investment, one tool will be the company's earnings, he said. "I don't have a concise plan because obviously I can't predict what the market's going to be and how much income, but it's definitely a priority of ours to take care of that preferred and at the same time to continue to deleverage and de-risk the business so that we can not only capitalize when the opportunity comes with lower rates," Ishbia said; this includes helping its brokers grow so every succeeds together. items.title: Deer Park Road launches MOF II to support non-agency RMBS
items.description: Deer Park Road launches MOF II to support non-agency RMBS By Donna M. Mitchell CloseText About Donna mailto donna.mitchell@arizent.com linkedin donnamitchellnj Published November 04, 2026, 12:58 p.m. EST | Updated November 04, 2026, 3:13 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Wavebreak Media for Adobe Stock Deer Park Road Management is preparing to launch a closed-end fund that will invest $2.5 billion investment in non-agency residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS), the company announced, to address reduced investor participation in the sector. Processing Content The Deer Park Mortgage Opportunity Fund II, or MOF II, will launch in January 2027 and begin investing as opportunities emerge that meet their underwriting criteria. MOF II addresses RMBS situations where "complexity, liquidity constraints and uncertainty around repayment timing can narrow the buyer base," according to sources familiar with the situation. Elevated interest rate volatility and increased pressure on non-agency RMBS valuations have also presented challenges to some investors, the company explained. Timing is another driving factor for Deer Park Road Management. The fund's predecessor, MOF I, will reach the end of its investment period in June 2027. During its three- and a half-year run, MOF I received $168 million in capital commitments, the company said. The valuation story In recent RMBS research, Deutsche Bank concurred with Deer Park Road's view on valuations, noting that non-residual yields on non-qualified mortgage bonds are being squeezed by the higher bond funding costs and have not been fully offset by higher mortgage rates. "Lower excess spread in deals should mean slightly higher credit enhancement and increases [in] interest shortfall risk," Deutsche Bank analysts wrote. Despite valuations being put under pressure, Deer Park Road Management said collateral fundamentals in some legacy securities is strong, making longer-term investor commitments, in the right security with the right execution, worthwhile. For certain non-agency RMBS higher rates, slower expected repayments, and wider mortgage spreads have squeezed valuations, even in cases where borrower credit is supported due to deleveraging, accumulated homeowner equity and structural credit protection, Deer Park Road said. ""We believe these securities can benefit from that disconnect by acquiring them at discounted prices and holding them as cash flows are realized," sources said. "MOF II's closed-end structure aligns the investment horizon with that process." Sustained investor confidence Deal sizes for new non-QM RMBS originations is growing, in another sign of confidence in the sector. New transactions with RMBS volumes of $1 billion or more are hitting the market again, and average deal sizes are approaching $500 million, Deutsche Bank Research said. The bank also noted that average deal sizes for home equity line-of-credit (HELOC) and closed-end second (CES) deals is stable, but the largest deals are seeing increases in how much they sell to investors. Some areas of non-agency RMBS are cooling, though. Single-family rental outstandings declined to $4 billion, from $58 billion in 2024. "Build-to-rent is the clearest path for a recovery in SFR issuance, but higher construction costs and bond funding costs stand in the way," Deutsche Bank said. Donna M. Mitchell Editor Donna M. Officials "will continue to put hardworking American's first with or without support from Democrats," he wrote. Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and Senate, which could make it easier for the party to advance legislation. They can also use hearings and investigations to press federal agencies and companies to answer for policies and practices that impact consumers, and exert leverage over confirmation of President Donald Trump's nominees. But turning campaign promises into changes people feel in their finances won't be easy. Trump can veto bills a Democrat-controlled Congress passes, limiting how much of their agenda could become law. Based on projections, Democrats will lack the numbers needed to override a presidential veto. watch now VIDEO 3:49 03:49 Democrats win 2026 midterms, pausing Trump agenda News Videos Any changes will also take time: Newly elected members of Congress won't take office until January. Here are eight ways Democrats’ new congressional majority could affect your money. 1. Healthcare "Not surprisingly, the Dems are going to be keyed in on affordability with respect to healthcare," said Zach Gaumer, vice president of health policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a nonpartisan think tank. Likely target areas include: ACA subsidies: Democrats could try to reinstate at least a portion of the enhanced premium subsidies for Affordable Care Act marketplace insurance plans, Gaumer said. Those enhanced subsidies expired at the end of 2025 , after the Republican-controlled Congress and Trump declined to extend them . Millions of ACA enrollees saw their monthly insurance premiums increase sharply as a result. Medicaid: Starting in 2027, states will be required to implement work requirements as a condition of Medicaid enrollment, due to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act the Republican-led Congress passed in 2025. Democrats will likely try to loosen those rules, and thereby avoid a large increase in the number of uninsured, Gaumer said. Long-term care: Medicare generally doesn't cover long-term care services, but Democrats may try to add some LTC coverage to the program's purview, Gaumer said. "That's an interest of several Democrats on the Hill right now," he said. 2. Taxes South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews answers questions from the audience during a campaign event at the Sandy Grove Missionary Baptist Church on October 21, 2026 in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. Andrews is running against Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC). Win Mcnamee | Getty Images OBBBA made Trump's 2017 tax cuts permanent and added temporary tax breaks. These included new deductions for tip income , overtime earnings , seniors and auto loan interest , which will expire after 2028 without an extension. Democrats may support extending these provisions. But as the Democrat-controlled Congress maps out its agenda, lawmakers will have to address the federal budget deficit. For fiscal year 2026, the budget deficit ballooned to nearly $2 trillion , the Treasury announced in October. Newly elected Democratic senators James Talarico of Texas, Troy Jackson of Maine and Annie Andrews of South Carolina all campaigned on expanding the child tax credit . Earlier this year, Senate Democrats also floated ideas to expand the standard deduction and create income tax exemptions for lower-earning Americans — which are costly proposals, according to Bunn from the Tax Foundation. "I've called these termites in the tax code," he said. "You cannot consistently narrow your base, especially for the income tax, and expect your spending priorities to be well-funded." 3. Student loans With Democrats in control of Congress, they are likely to hold hearings and subpoena Trump officials over the administration's student loan policies, said higher education expert Mark Kantrowitz. One priority may be pressing the Education Department to fix the popular Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, which cancels the remaining federal student debt of eligible government and nonprofit workers after a decade. Over the summer, Trump officials reassessed repayment timelines, delaying some borrowers' forgiveness date by years. Broad student loan forgiveness is unlikely: Trump could veto such a bill, and the Supreme Court blocked the Biden administration's plan. More attainable changes could include restoring tax-free treatment of forgiven student debt, raising the new borrowing caps and expanding repayment options — measures that may attract bipartisan support, Kantrowitz said. items.title: Punk (Noir) Is Dead. What Did Dallas Miss?
items.description: Punk (Noir) Is Dead. What Did Dallas Miss? {{ imageOneIndex }} / {{ imageCount }} Advertisement Related Content Doesn’t sound like graffiti and metal spikes, does it? Maybe this dissonance was one of the fissures under the McKeel family’s feet. Perhaps people heard “punk” and expected drinks set on fire and food dyed black. Others might have known about the punk community’s prominent vein of vegetarianism and veganism . “For us,” John says, “[punk] simply meant that we wanted to break the rules, have a little edge, make the restaurant something that you didn’t see someplace else.” Cole adds, “It was never about being a rock-and-roll restaurant.” There were a few mind-bending moments. Cooper’s “banana split” dessert was a spectacular flavor combination of banana, miso, and mole rojo ice cream. Corn agnolotti pasta promised to be all sweetness and light, but aggressive slices of compressed Fresno chile pepper were hidden underneath. The twists may not be over. As this article went to press in late October, Cooper was trying to raise funds to open his own unpunk restaurant in the space. The McKeel family, though, was still reeling from their financial and emotional losses, certain that Dallas had just rejected their dream. “I’m sad for Dallas,” John says. “I hope that somebody else picks up the mantle and runs with it. I’m just afraid that maybe this is going to scare other tasting menu-style restaurants from wanting to stretch their legs.” The family’s vision of a new style of fine dining is dead. They debate theories about what killed it. Did they choose the wrong location? The wrong chef? Was the restaurant too big? Is Dallas not interested in fine dining , punk, or the specific combination of the two? Could the McKeels have better marketed the more affordable menus or what, exactly, “punk” meant to them? Was it too punk or not punk enough? The answer may have been all of the above. Punk Noir was fascinating, an experience far more earnest and familial than it appeared. items.title: Ballot roulette: Florida voters pick property tax break over local services
items.description: With the cost of living on the ballot, Florida voters approved a major tax break for homeowners. The amendment to increase the Sunshine State's homestead exemption won the 60% it needed on election night. Voters weren't swayed by warnings that the higher exemption would devastate municipal coffers and services. The ballot measure was given little chance of winning. But current economic conditions proved an insurmountable obstacle for the argument against the measure. Unofficial returns showed it finishing with 62% of the vote. The changes take effect in phases starting in 2027. "An incredible victory for Florida homeowners!" the Florida Republican Party wrote on social media . "More money stays in your pocket." Neil Schiller, managing partner at Government Law Group , told HousingWire TBD the result will change how cities weigh development. "Projects that generate jobs, economic activity, and alternative tax revenues may become more attractive, while developments that require significant public services and infrastructure will face greater financial scrutiny," Schiller said. "Amendment 3 may be remembered as the moment Florida cities had to fundamentally reinvent how they do business." The vote shows how important affordability has become, Andrew Hellinger, co-principal at Urban-X Group , developer of River Landing Shops & Residences in Miami, said in an e-mail to HousingWire TBD . Hellinger added, "However, people still need roads, public transportation and essential community services, and those have to be paid for." What the exemption does The amendment replaces the $50,000 homestead exemption with a phased increase. It rises to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Only primary residences qualify, so second-home and investment-property owners get nothing. Homeowners must establish Florida residency by Dec. 31, 2026, to get the full benefit. Later arrivals get the $50,000 exemption for four years before qualifying. The school board levy is excluded. The measure also cuts the annual assessment cap on non-homestead commercial property from 10% to 5%. That change starts Jan. 1, 2027. Renters, who occupy about a third of Florida's housing units, get no relief. How Florida got here Gov. Ron DeSantis called a special session to put the amendment on the ballot. Lawmakers approved it with changes protecting school funding. DeSantis had sought a broader exemption. DeSantis cast the measure as a fix for tax bills inflated by pandemic-era migration. Newcomers, led by New Yorkers, overwhelmed the housing supply and lifted values and tax burdens for longtime residents. Florida home prices rose more than 50% between 2020 and 2022. Prices have since stalled, and the average home value fell 3.7% over the past year. Assessments haven't followed: under the Save Our Homes recapture rule, they keep rising until they meet market value. The annual increase is capped at 3% or inflation, whichever is less. Most counties held millage rates steady or cut them, yet bills still climbed. City tax bills statewide rose about 50% on average over several years. Voters heard the warnings The Florida Sheriffs Association said in August it was "significantly concerned." By mid-September, it was running ads featuring sheriffs from four counties. One said, "We want a tax cut too, but Amendment 3 is the wrong way to do it." Association President Billy Woods warned of fewer deputies, slower 911 response and more crime. Opponents also included the Florida State Fraternal Order of Police , Florida Professional Firefighters and Florida Fire Chiefs Association . The Florida League of Cities and Florida Association of Counties opposed it, citing too much uncertainty. According to the legislature's economic research office, estimated local governments would lose nearly $5 billion in 2027-28. The Florida Policy Institute, a progressive think tank, created Floridians for Shared Prosperity, which sponsored a campaign urging a no vote. "Amendment 3 will leave working families and seniors with a lose-lose choice: pay more through new fees and higher taxes or face major cuts to the services you depend on," the campaign’s website stated. Voters approved the amendment anyway, with encouragement from the Florida Realtors and others in real estate. “This is your one shot at real property tax relief,” apartment owner and investor Grant Washington wrote on social media Monday. “Vote Yes on Amendment 3 and put your money back where it belongs. In your pocket!” Related More: Florida Property Tax

items.title: NAR advances strategic plan with new tools, MLS outreach and housing initiatives
items.description: The National Association of Realtors (NAR) is moving from policy wins to implementation as it rolls out fraud-prevention tools, MLS engagement and housing supply efforts tied to its 2026–2028 strategic plan , according to a third-quarter progress report released Wednesday. The update, covering the quarter ended Sept. 30, outlines how NAR is trying to convert advocacy wins and market research into practical support for agents, brokers and MLSs as the industry adjusts to commission lawsuits, changing rules and tighter housing affordability. NAR said its work in the third quarter focused on five areas: MLS engagement, executing new federal housing-supply law , fraud prevention, commercial market intelligence and broker support. The association also highlighted technology and data initiatives, as well as developments in ongoing antitrust litigation. MLS engagement ramps up amid rule changes NAR said it has now “expanded MLS executive engagement ” to nearly 500 MLS leaders and formed a new MLS work group made up of industry experts. The group is publishing resources focused on maintaining a “pro-competitive, transparent marketplace,” according to the association’s update. The outreach sits on top of an ongoing feedback effort that includes surveys, focus groups and in-person meetings with members, NAR said. Why it matters: MLSs are reassessing rules, data access and listing practices in light of settlement-driven policy changes and regulatory scrutiny. More structured engagement between NAR and MLSs could influence how quickly and consistently local marketplaces adapt and how much operational risk brokers face during the transition. Implementation work begins on new housing law NAR’s report puts significant emphasis on follow-through after the passage of the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act , which became law July 11. The association said it “spearheaded” the push for the bill and is now working with state and local associations to turn the federal statute into local supply and affordability gains. Beyond the ROAD to Housing Act, NAR said it continued advocacy for the More Homes on the Market Act and secured another “ credit score modernization ” change at the Federal Housing Administration. Details on the FHA move were not included in the high-level summary. Why it matters: With mortgage rates still elevated and inventory tight in many markets, the near-term impact of any federal housing law will depend on how quickly local governments change zoning, permitting and infrastructure processes. Lenders, builders and brokers should watch how NAR and its state partners translate the law into specific local reforms and incentives. Fraud-prevention hub responds to rising scams NAR launched a central fraud-prevention hub and a consumer-facing guide aimed at helping members, associations and buyers and sellers spot red flags, protect sensitive information and safeguard transactions. The association also rolled out new fraud- and AI-focused education, including NAR NXT conference sessions and a Broker Power Hour on AI voice cloning and deepfake scams. Why it matters: Wire fraud, business email compromise and emerging AI-enabled scams are driving higher operational and reputational risk on transactions. Centralized resources and training from NAR could influence how brokerages standardize verification, identity and communication protocols at the office level. Commercial members get new demand index, dashboards For commercial practitioners, NAR launched the Commercial Real Estate Demand Index and expanded the members-only Metro Market Dashboard. The association also released six local market assessment reports intended to give commercial Realtors a clearer view of where demand is growing across major property types. Why it matters : With office valuations under pressure and higher rates reshaping cap rates, local demand data can help investors, lenders and brokers price risk, underwrite deals and identify resilient sectors within each metro. Broker engagement and education initiatives grow NAR said it connected with more than 5,000 brokers in the quarter to discuss business challenges and share broker-focused resources. It also expanded broker programming and peer engagement, including a national broker networking session and planning for the first Broker Innovation Forum, scheduled for the NAR NXT conference. The association said it is also building out data, technology and security resources, including expanded AI and emerging technology programming and new member research via the 2026 Realtors Technology Report, which tracks how agents are using tools in their businesses. Additional third-quarter highlights cited by NAR include: Federal appeals courts upholding dismissals in the Eytalis and Homie antitrust cases Publication of a Data Center Impact Report Groundwork for a December launch of a modernized learning platform and courses Why it matters: For brokerage leaders and MLS executives, NAR’s education and technology agenda will shape what agents are trained on — from AI usage to compliance — and may influence which tools and workflows firms prioritize heading into the 2027 market cycle. NAR’s third-quarter update is part of a standing reporting cadence on its 2026–2028 strategic plan, which is organized around expanding housing opportunity, protecting market integrity and delivering business-building resources for members. items.title: The mortgage operating model after AI
items.description: In my previous two articles, I explored why the mortgage industry's biggest AI challenge is structural and how the traditional brokerage operating model creates complexity as businesses grow . That brings us to a more fundamental question: If we could redesign mortgage origination around what AI now makes possible, what would we build? Today, the process is organized around a series of narrowly defined roles and handoffs, with loan officers, assistants, processors, underwriters and others each responsible for moving the file to the next stage. Every handoff creates another opportunity for information to get lost and responsibility to be pushed downstream. I believe the mortgage operating model of the future will be organized around a persistent, provable understanding of the borrower and the lifecycle of the loan, rather than the people, systems and handoffs that define the process today. Start with an evidence-based picture of the borrower At its core, a mortgage involves building an evidence-based profile of an individual and applying a risk model to it. Today, that profile is repeatedly reconstructed or revalidated by originators, lenders, underwriters and other participants because each has limited visibility into, or confidence in, the work that came before. Imagine instead a persistent, evidence-backed borrower profile that brings together information from pay stubs, tax returns, credit reports and other sources, with each data point retaining a verifiable connection to its original evidence. That includes where the information came from and how it was calculated, interpreted or reconciled with other information. The result would be a more complete and transparent understanding of the borrower that persists throughout the loan lifecycle. Rather than reconstructing that information each time another party needs to assess the loan, participants could trace the underlying evidence, understand how previous conclusions were reached and build on the work already performed, while still conducting their own necessary evaluations and verifications. Apply different risk models to the same underlying evidence To be sure, understanding the borrower is only part of the equation. Every lender, agency and mortgage product has its own requirements and risk criteria. Today, those requirements are translated into guidelines, matrices and documents that must be interpreted and applied by people across multiple stages of the origination process. With a common, verifiable borrower profile, different risk models could be applied to the same underlying information. A system could evaluate how Fannie Mae , Freddie Mac or a particular lender would assess the borrower, identify missing evidence and determine what needs to happen next. Specialized AI agents could then coordinate and execute much of that work, from collecting documents and preparing calculations to addressing conditions and identifying exceptions that require human review. Consider how often a missing document or unresolved discrepancy surfaces late in the process, forcing a loan officer or processor to revisit work that should have been completed weeks earlier. With a more complete understanding of the borrower and the requirements of the loan, those agents could identify many of those issues earlier, coordinate the necessary follow-up and maintain an auditable record of the work performed. The implications extend beyond making individual tasks faster to changing how information is maintained and how work gets done, creating an opportunity to rethink the organization itself. When the loan carries the context, the organization can change When technology maintains the evidence, context and requirements throughout the loan lifecycle, people no longer need to serve as the connective tissue between every task and system. Specialized AI agents can increasingly handle work traditionally distributed across different roles, while experienced mortgage professionals oversee execution, validate results and exercise judgment. Consider the processor, whose role could evolve from coordinating documents, conditions and handoffs to overseeing the quality and performance of the loan process. Specialized AI agents could collect documents, prepare calculations and track conditions, while the processor sets standards, validates results, resolves exceptions and continuously improves the workflow. This shift would also change how mortgage organizations define and reward expertise. Rather than measuring success by the number of people someone manages or the tasks they complete, organizations could focus on accurate files, predictable closings, borrower experience and ultimately, a lower cost to originate. By reducing manual handoffs and repetitive work, experienced professionals could oversee more loans without a corresponding increase in staffing. The result would be a mortgage organization structured around the lifecycle of the loan rather than inherited job descriptions. Instead of scaling by adding more people to manage each stage of origination, companies could build teams around broader accountability for the loan from application to funding, with AI supporting the work required along the way. What it all means Origination is the logical place to prove this model because it is where the borrower's evidence is first assembled and evaluated. But once a provable, evidence-based profile exists, its usefulness could extend well beyond funding. Other participants across the mortgage value chain, including investors and capital markets firms, could eventually apply their own risk models to the same underlying information, allowing for more granular risk assessment without repeatedly reconstructing the loan. My prediction is that AI will reshape not only mortgage organizations , but also how they work together. items.title: Nationwide Equities debuts ReverseReach tool for mortgage broker lead generation help
items.description: Nationwide Equities Corp. has launched ReverseReach, a new tool and support program aimed at helping mortgage brokers and loan officers uncover reverse mortgage opportunities in their existing customer databases and referral networks, the company announced Tuesday. The New Jersey-based wholesale reverse mortgage lender said ReverseReach is designed for originators who may not specialize in reverse products but have years of past customers who are now older, equity rich and potential candidates for reverse mortgages. “ Mortgage brokers may be sitting on substantial untapped business opportunities without even realizing it,” Paul Lamparillo, CEO of Nationwide Equities , said in a statement. “Over the years, brokers have built relationships with thousands of homeowners, many of whom may now qualify for reverse mortgage products. "We created ReverseReach to make uncovering those highly lucrative opportunities simple, efficient and accessible — even for brokers who have never closed a reverse mortgage before — so they can confidently and comfortably begin originating them.” The company has largely pivoted to proprietary reverse mortgage production, mirroring recent changes in the broader industry. Modex data shows that Nationwide Equities has originated 111 reverse mortgages for $216 million in volume over the past 12 months, while data compiled by Reverse Market Insight shows that it has endorsed 26 Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) through the first nine months of this year. In 2020, Nationwide Equities launched its private-label reverse mortgage, EquityPower , which was built to offer higher loan proceeds than HECM products. How ReverseReach works ReverseReach allows mortgage professionals to enter a borrower’s financial and property scenario and quickly gauge whether a reverse mortgage is worth pursuing. The program is positioned as a preliminary opportunity identification tool rather than a full underwriting engine. Key features include: A scenario runner that lets originators input basic borrower and property data to see if a reverse mortgage may be viable Targeting homeowners age 55 and older, including those with limited qualifying income or constrained access to traditional refinance options A focus on borrowers looking to improve monthly cash flow by removing required principal and interest payments Support for borrowers facing financial stress who may not fit conventional underwriting Regardless of the initial result, brokers can connect with a live underwriter to discuss the file and potential structures, according to the company. Live underwriting help desk Nationwide Equities is pairing the technology with a help desk staffed by full-time Direct Endorsement (DE) underwriters who answer eligibility questions, help structure loans and walk brokers through complex borrower situations . “One of the biggest obstacles to broader reverse mortgage adoption is simply recognizing when a borrower may be a good candidate,” Philip Parziale, president of Nationwide Equities said in a statement. “ReverseReach bridges that gap. Brokers don't need to become reverse mortgage experts to identify a potential transaction. They need a simple way to recognize the opportunity and a knowledgeable lending partner to help them execute it.” Parziale added that direct access to underwriters is a central part of the offering. “Regardless of how good your technology is, there is something special about being able to speak to a live person on the phone and walk you through a scenario and respond to follow ups,” he said. Use cases and business development The launch comes as volume in the broader forward mortgage market remains under pressure from higher rates, tighter affordability and intense competition for a smaller pool of qualified borrowers. Many retail and broker shops are looking to diversify into reverse mortgages, home equity products or nonqualified mortgages (non-QM) to stabilize production. For brokers, the reverse space has historically been constrained by product complexity, reputation concerns and training requirements. ReverseReach aims to lower that barrier by giving originators a simple screening workflow across their existing loan origination system and past client lists, backed by lender-side expertise. Lenders are investing in education and simple tools to capture aging-in-place demand from older homeowners with significant home equity. Brokers who have closed thousands of loans over the past decade may find that a meaningful share of these clients now meet age and equity thresholds for reverse products. Nationwide Equities positions ReverseReach as a business development strategy focused on reengaging existing borrowers rather than purchasing new leads or ramping up paid marketing . Potential applications include: Mining closed-loan databases for borrowers with strong equity positions who are now 55 or older Reviewing files for clients who have struggled with debt -to-income ratios in past forward refinance scenarios Partnering with financial advisers or real estate agents to flag older homeowners needing payment relief or cash-flow support Related More: Mortgage Broker Nationwide Equities Reverse Mortgage Daily Technology

items.title: Absolute Home Mortgage targets growth through First Option strategic transaction
items.description: Absolute Home Mortgage Corp. on Wednesday announced a strategic transaction with First Option Mortgage that positions the combined independent mortgage bank to grow its originations volume. The move was not considered to be a merger or acquisition. New Jersey-based Absolute said in its announcement that Georgia-based First Option will migrate onto Absolute’s platform and continue to operate as a DBA unit after regulatory approval. The deal also brings First Option executives into Absolute’s ownership and governance structure, a move aimed at building out a dedicated growth engine in a consolidating market . As part of the transaction, First Option leaders Alvin Shah and Kurt Nikolai will join Absolute’s ownership group and board of directors, pending regulatory approval. Shah will become chief strategy officer, with responsibility for strategic expansion and additional acquisitions that are actively pursuing, according to the announcement. Combined with Absolute’s wholly owned subsidiary Mortgage Equity Partners , the platform is “positioned to originate approximately $4 billion annually” once approvals are complete, the company said. That level of volume would give the lender additional operating leverage at a time when many independent mortgage banks (IMBs) are looking to scale up or sell. “This partnership is exciting. We have proven what we can do together in the face of adversity and tough market conditions,” Matthew VanFossen , CEO of Absolute Home Mortgage Corp, said in a statement. “Now we are 100% confident that we are strategically positioned to scale. There is no better time to capitalize on the foundation we have built.” Data from Modex shows that Absolute Home Mortgage has closed roughly 3,000 loans and $1.13 billion in volume over the past 12 months, with 250 producing loan officers across 33 branches. First Option has produced $398 million across 1,300-plus units and has 91 producing LOs across 11 branches. Massachusetts-based Mortgage Equity Partners has 81 producing LOs across 19 branches, with total volume of $613 million on nearly 1,600 loans in the past year. Leadership and structure Absolute said Shah, Nikolai and VanFossen have worked in “close strategic alignment” for years, operating separate IMBs but maintaining similar approaches to operating models, culture and growth. Bringing these businesses and teams under one platform formalizes the relationship. “We have been building toward this for years, on the operating model, on the culture and on the vision,” Nikolai said in a statement. “We have been strategically aligned for years, and we have seen firsthand how well our teams work together. Bringing our two lenders together makes natural sense.” The First Option team will keep its existing leadership and sales culture while continuing to serve borrowers and referral partners in local markets under a DBA structure. That approach mirrors how some companies are structuring IMB rollups — centralized capital, compliance and operations paired with local branding and relationships. Building an acquisition platform Absolute framed the deal as another step in a longer-term consolidation strategy. The company said it intends to continue acquiring and partnering with independent mortgage companies that want to gain scale while retaining their brands and leadership teams. Shah said the combined platform is designed to be attractive to other IMBs facing higher costs, thinner margins and increasing compliance demands. “I am excited about the combined resources of this team and the scaling opportunity it brings to the market,” Shah said. “Scale creates opportunities for other mortgage companies to join our platform and become more profitable. We have the people, the capital alignment and the platform to grow aggressively, and we intend to.” VanFossen said he expects scale and customer retention to be critical in the next cycle. “The IMBs that win the next cycle will be the ones that operate at scale, retain their customers, and move decisively when the market opens up,” he said. “That is exactly what we are building. First Option is a major step, and we are not done. We intend to be the platform of choice for independent lenders who want to grow.” Related More: Lenders Partnerships

items.title: The midterms are shaping the housing policy landscape. What real estate pros should watch
items.description: The 2026 midterm elections saw the election of several legislators and policies that could have a large impact on housing and finance policy in the U.S. Heading into Tuesday’s election, which saw both branches of Congress flip from Republican to Democratic control, the National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn identified 37 competitive races in the U.S. House and nine competitive U.S. Senate races. “Regardless of which party controls Congress, NAR’s priorities remain the same: increasing housing supply, improving affordability, protecting property rights and expanding access to homeownership,” McGahn told HousingWire in an emailed statement. “Our research shows that 85% of Americans believe homeownership is part of the American Dream, underscoring why housing must remain a priority for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.” McGahn noted that candidates supported by the Realtors Political Action Committee (RPAC) won in at least 325 races, with additional results still coming in. "The historic bipartisan passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act demonstrated what Congress can accomplish when lawmakers work together,” McGahn, a 2024 HousingWire Woman of Influence , said. “We will continue building on that momentum, working with Realtor champions and real estate allies in both parties to advance commonsense solutions that bring more homes to the market and help more Americans achieve the dream of homeownership.” From congressional races that could shift the direction of federal housing policy to newly elected governors promising to tackle housing shortages, the election results could have significant implications for the real estate industry. Voters also weighed in on ballot measures addressing property taxes, down payment assistance and housing development. Here’s a look at the key races and measures. House races NAR was watching Three races NAR was closely watching were for U.S. House seats in New Jersey. In the state’s Fourth District, Christopher Smith, the republican incumbent representative won reelection. He has held the seat since 1981. Smith’s housing policy stance focuses primarily on veteran homelessness and permanent supportive housing programs, while emphasizing local control and affordability support. In New Jersey’s 11th District, Analilia Mejia, the democratic incumbent, also won reelection. Mejia is known for her support of the Homes for All Act. She campaigned on a progressive platform focused on expanding public housing supply, curbing corporate ownership of residential properties and providing tax relief for first-time buyers. The third race NAR was watching was in New Jersey’s Seventh District, which saw Democrat Rebecca Bennett beat out incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Kean. In her campaign, Bennett promised to lead efforts to cut the red tape on building efforts working to increase housing supply. In Wisconsin, Rep. Scott Fitzgerald, a republican, won reelection. During his time in office, he has introduced a package of bills addressing housing finance and construction costs. One proposal would create a financing program intended to help developers build more housing for middle-income households — while others address Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and mortgage processing. Over in Colorado, as of early Wednesday afternoon, it appeared that Eileen Laubacher would be successful in flipping the state’s fourth district seat, beating out incumbent Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert. Laubacher has promised to fight to keep foreign entities out of Colorado land ownership. Boebert has pushed for mortgage underwriting and credit score reform, which she has claimed will allow more qualified Americans to buy homes. States seek affordable housing champions California’s closely watched gubernatorial race was won by Democrat Xavier Becerra. During his campaign, Becerra said he plans to declare a housing-shortage state of emergency on his first day as governor. Through this, he said he would create a dedicated team to coordinate efforts to increase housing supply with local governments and developers. Some of the things he is focused on include a framework to unify zoning, fee structures, regulatory costs and financing targets, which he believes will enable median-income families to afford median-priced homes. He is also looking to expand state mortgage and down-payment assistance programs for renters and will encourage infill development near public transport. In Ohio, the race for governor was won by Democratic candidate Amy Acton. During her campaign, Acton proposed expanding the state’s Welcome Home Ohio program to support new construction. He has also said he is looking to streamline the permit review proce ss and reduce local parking minimums. items.title: The morning after the midterms: Why every agent should be on the phone today and what to say
items.description: Last night, Democrats flipped both the House and the Senate. This morning, every person in your database woke up, read the headlines, and had the same thought: “What does this mean for my house?” They are going to get an answer to that question today. The only question is who gives it to them. It will be their brother-in-law, a cable news panel, a social media feed engineered to make them anxious, or you. If you are a real estate professional, and you do anything today before you pick up the phone and call your database, you have your priorities backward. I have been coaching agents for more than 40 years and through nine presidential and midterm cycles. I can tell you with certainty what happens over the next two weeks. A portion of your buyers will quietly pause. A portion of your sellers will wonder if they should pull their listing. Investors will start reading tax rumors. And agents who stay quiet will lose those people, not to a competitor, but to indecision. Indecision is the real competitor this week. Why the call matters more than the content Here is what most agents miss: the client does not need you to be an economist . They need you to be calm, reachable and first. A three-minute call that says “I’m not calling about anything, I just know people are wondering what this means for real estate , so I’m checking in,” does three things no email can do. First, it positions you as the trusted source before the noise gets there. Second, it surfaces warm leads. Anyone who asks a real question about buying, selling or refinancing today is telling you they are thinking about a move. Third, it reminds every person in your database that you exist, which, if we are honest, is the single biggest reason agents lose repeat and referral business . The call is not a pitch. Do not sell. Do not share your politics, even if they share theirs; half your database voted the other way. Listen, answer briefly and get off the phone with a reason to call again in 60 days. Then log every conversation. The questions you will hear, and how to answer them Below are the questions agents are already fielding this morning, with answers that are honest, neutral, and short. Use them as a starting point and put them in your own words. “Are mortgage rates going up or down because of the election?” Rates follow inflation, jobs data, and the 10-year Treasury, not election returns. Markets opened higher this morning, and the Federal Reserve meets in December, which will move rates far more than Tuesday did. Nobody knows the direction with certainty, which is exactly why timing the market is a losing game. Be sure to subscribe to HousingWire's daily news podcast, HousingWire Daily , where you can get daily economic housing intelligence. “Are home prices going to crash?” There is no sign of that. Prices are set by supply and demand, and most markets still have more buyers than homes. A new Congress does not change how many houses exist on your street. “Should I wait to buy until things settle down?” “Settled down” never arrives. Every year has a reason to wait. The people who bought during the last three election cycles are sitting on equity; the people who waited are paying more rent. If a home fits your life and your budget, the calendar matters more than the Capitol. “Should I wait to sell?” Same logic in reverse. Spring brings more buyers but also more competition. Right now you are selling against fewer listings, and the buyers who are out the week after an election are serious. Let’s look at what is actually on the market in your neighborhood this week and decide with numbers, not headlines. “With Democrats taking Congress, what changes for housing?” Realistically, not much soon. We now have a divided government, which means major legislation is unlikely for the next two years. Any housing bill you hear about would take months or years to pass and longer to reach your street. I will let you know if anything real moves. “What about my property taxes, the SALT deduction or capital gains?” Any tax change has to pass both chambers and be signed by the President, so nothing happens overnight. If a specific proposal gains traction, I will flag it, and that becomes a conversation with your CPA before you make any decision about your home. “Is the economy going to tank?” The stock market’s first reaction this morning was positive. Beyond that, anyone who gives you a confident forecast is guessing. What history shows is that real estate has been the most stable asset people own through every administration of either party. “Is this a good time to refinance?” That depends on your current rate , not on the election. Tell me what you are paying, and I will have a lender run the numbers, no obligation. Rates could drift either way in the coming months, so it is worth knowing your threshold now. “I’m an investor. Does this change anything?” Not today. Rents and vacancy rates do not care about Congress. Keep an eye on any discussion of 1031 exchanges or depreciation rules, but those are long-shot, multi-year conversations. There is nothing to react to this week. “Should I pull my house off the market?” Only if your reason for selling has changed. The casual buyers are home watching the news. The ones still touring homes this week mean it. “Where should I get accurate information?” From me and from your lender, not from your social media feed. I will call you if something actually changes. The real risk this week The danger after any election is not the policy. It is the paralysis. items.title: NIMBYs cite a 155-year-old law to thwart a San Francisco project
items.description: California state lawmakers have spent years tilting the rules toward new housing. Projects that meet fixed standards can skip public hearings, and cities that say no face legal and financial risk. Still, muncipal and local neighborhood opponents never seem to run out of ways to try to scuttle projects. A Northern California federal court is embroiled in one of the latest examples. In San Francisco, one of the most expensive housing cities in the world, opponents of an 848-unit residential structure above an existing Safeway grocery store have escalated to a new level. They invoked the Civil Rights Act of 1871, a law passed to protect Black Americans from Ku Klux Klan violence, when they sued the city in September. Assembly Bill 2011 is increasingly at the center of these disputes. The 2022 state law lets qualifying projects on commercially zoned land skip public hearings and environmental review. Lawmakers broadened it last year, while community opposition groups keep probing its edges . Neighbors and other opponents argue that the Safeway project doesn't qualify for the shortcut. They claim the city shut them out of the process. Last week, the Marina Safeway developer's lawyers asked the court to dismiss the suit. The filing called the opposition's tactic "a deeper perversion" of a law meant to protect Black Americans from Klan violence. They argue that civil rights statutes exist to protect victims of discrimination, not to serve as "a weapon" for one of San Francisco's "most well-resourced communities" to block new home development. The project and the lawsuit The developers' plan would replace the Safeway at 15 Marina Blvd. and its parking lot with 848 homes. Eighty-six would be for lower-income households. The homes would rise in towers of 22 and 18 stories above a newly built grocery store at ground level. The site is zoned for 40 feet. California AB 2011 instructs city planners to check only that the plans meet fixed rules. San Francisco declared the project eligible Aug. 13. In response, YesAnd Foundation, Neighborhoods United SF and four residents sued Sept. 11 in federal court in San Francisco. The defendants named are the city, its planning and public health directors, and PG&E . PG&E once operated a power plant on the site. Align Real Estate and Marina Property Owner LLC are named as real parties in interest. The complaint says the plaintiffs "support the creation of housing generally." It accuses city planners of "rubber-stamping" a project that doesn't qualify. Invoking a Klan-era law comes in The neighbors' only federal claim says the permitting and approval shortcut denied them a public hearing, violating their due process rights. They filed the case under Section 1983, part of a 1871 law. It is the only claim that qualifies the case for federal court. Their other six claims arise under California law. Holland & Knight , the developer's firm, argues that civil rights laws have long been "powerless" to undo the effects of the housing shortage. The state's own housing law says the crisis has caused "discrimination against low-income and minority households." The brief says California has finally moved to end its pattern of privileging existing homeowners over people who need housing. The neighbors, it argues, want to use civil rights law "not to protect the victims of discrimination." It says Section 1983 targeted a Klan "campaign of violence and deception," quoting a 1985 Supreme Court ruling. The brief also cites a 2008 Ninth Circuit ruling that rejected a similar claim from neighbors in Spokane. That court held neighbors have no constitutional right to a hearing on someone else's permit. The brief argues that accepting the claim would turn every ministerial approval into a potential federal lawsuit. A toxic-site dispute But the plaintiffs also turned to a more common approach in fighting projects. They argue there are environmental dangers . The Safeway sits on the site of an old PG&E steam plant, next to a former coal-gas plant. A state toxics official told city planners in December 2025 she didn't expect the site "to qualify for streamlined approval." She cited 2023 petroleum readings 10 times the residential screening level. In 2024, the regional Water Board, the lead regulator, closed the cleanup of petroleum from the steam plant. It found "no unacceptable public health risks for the current land use." That finding rested on the store's commercial use, and the board said it "may reconsider" if the use changes. The neighbors say the city approved the project before anyone sampled soil beneath the store. In February, the complaint says, the developer's consultant acknowledged "a data gap." The consultant said Safeway would not allow drilling while the store operates. The developer's lawyers say AB 2011 requires cleanup only before the city issues a certificate of occupancy. The neighbors argue that full contamination assessment must come first. Questioning filing in federal court The brief says state law now strongly favors housing. It cites the Housing Accountability Act, which it says requires courts to give "the fullest possible weight" to approving homes. Under that law, it argues, a city's finding can be overturned only if no reasonable person could have reached it. The developer’s attorneys target the lawsuit's placement in federal court. Federal courts can't issue the California-style court orders the neighbors want, they argue. If the federal claim fails, they contend, the case belongs in state court. Their brief notes no California court has yet interpreted AB 2011. U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín will hear the motion Feb. 4, 2027. Related More: Housing Policy San Francisco

items.title: D.C. Mayor-Elect Wants Options Beyond Therme's $550M Spa Proposal
items.description: D.C. Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George is keeping her options open for what could anchor Poplar Point, the District’s last major waterfront development opportunity. Lewis George won the mayoral race Tuesday night and is set to take the reins from Mayor Muriel Bowser, who will step down from her nearly 12-year run in January. Bowser’s administration has been pushing a proposal to anchor Poplar Point with a $550M thermal bathing retreat from Therme Group . On Wednesday, Lewis George said she doesn’t want to preclude other development opportunities that could better meet the needs of D.C. residents. “I don't want to foreclose proposals by declaring that Therme is what's going to be there,” she said at a press conference. “Therme is welcome to continue to try to be one of the anchors and partners there, but I don't want to move forward in foreclosing those opportunities.” Wikimedia Commons/Council of the District of Columbia Janeese Lewis George, photographed in September 2023 Poplar Point, a 110-acre parkland on the eastern bank of the Anacostia River, has long been envisioned as a future mixed-use waterfront neighborhood like Navy Yard or The Wharf. Over the past few years, the Bowser administration has accelerated efforts to kick-start the redevelopment project. And in 2025, it selected Therme as the anchor. Before Bowser's term ends, her administration has sought to finalize two key pieces of legislation that would move Poplar Point and Therme’s proposed spa forward. But Lewis George told The Washington Sun last month that she has concerns about the project and that the site should be used to build more affordable homes. The mayor-elect on Wednesday said the city “needs to put the people of the District of Columbia first” in all the deals it makes. “We want people to say, ‘Hey, we want to be on Poplar Point. We're willing to build X, Y and Z. We're willing to show up for the residents and give these many amenities,’” Lewis George said. She committed in her mayoral campaign to building 72,000 new homes , speeding up development of affordable homes and modernizing rent stabilization. She reiterated her pledge to focus on affordability and said she hopes to “show real impact” in her first year in office. “I feel confident that we can deliver on universal access to childcare, that we can rein in our utility companies and deliver more affordability as it relates to utilities for our city and, of course, that we can make it easier for people to build homes in the city, to build more homes so we can lower the cost,” she said. items.title: Deutsche Finance Offices Raided In Connection With BVK's U.S. Real Estate Investments
items.description: The offices of Deutsche Finance in Munich were raided by the Munich Public Prosecutor’s office as part of an investigation involving massive losses on a U.S. real estate portfolio into which Bayerische Versorgungskammer , the German pension fund better known as BVK, poured nearly $2B. Unsplash/Compagnons Deutsche Finance confirmed the raid was carried out on Tuesday in a brief statement that says it was searched as a “third party” to the case, that it was cooperating with authorities and that it “has been in contact with them for some time.” Deutsche Finance America filed a lawsuit in September against BVK in Delaware Superior Court for breach of contract, defamation, deceptive trade practices and a host of other claims related to its alleged mismanagement of the real estate porfolio that led to more than $1B in losses. BVK invested $1.9B in seven projects through a partnership with Deutsche Finance America and developer Michael Shvo , whose real estate empire has been battered by lawsuits and shed its core assets. The portfolio included San Francisco’s Transamerica Pyramid , which Shvo 's eponymous development firm sold for $691M in April at a loss for the ownership group that had poured more than $1B into the iconic tower. Shvo also sold the site of the historic Raleigh Hotel in Miami Beach in October 2025 after a plan to rehabilitate and redevelop the property into a $2B project collapsed amid poor sales . Other Shvo projects, like a Mandarin Oriental condo tower in Manhattan, drew high-profile complaints at the same time that the developer was engaged in a scathing legal battle with private club operator Core Club over a planned location in the Transamerica Pyramid. BVK, Germany’s largest pension fund, said in February that its total losses from the investments with Shvo exceeded $1B and that it was looking to exit its relationship with the developer. Other assets in the portfolio included the Mandarin Oriental Residences in Beverly Hills and the Coca-Cola building in Manhattan. In its September lawsuit, Deutsche Finance alleged that BVK’s mismanagement of the U.S. portfolio included failing to provide oversight on operating budgets, refinancing decisions and proposed leases. BVK misled Deutsche Finance about its involvement in the investments and hid that it controlled leasing, construction, financing, pricing and capital decisions at the projects, the suit says. BVK firmly rejected the allegations at the time and said they constituted “an obvious attempt by Deutsche Finance to divert attention from its own responsibility and its numerous, publicly known challenges.” The losses at BVK have drawn attention across Germany, including from investigators, Bloomberg reported . The pension fund oversees $137B in retirement assets for 2.8 million people. items.title: Texas Flips Blue, Putting Data Center Boom On Notice
items.description: Texas elected Democrats to its top offices for the first time in decades, a move that could ripple through the burgeoning data center industry across the state. X/Gina Hinojosa Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico Gina Hinojosa was named the projected winner for Texas governor, and James Talarico was named the projected winner for U.S. Senate on Tuesday night by The Associated Press. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott , the 12-year Republican incumbent, said he called Hinojosa to concede at about 10 p.m. CT Tuesday. Hinojosa had more than 4.4 million votes , or 53%, with 80% of Texas counties reporting late Tuesday, compared to about 3.8 million votes for Abbott. The 52-year-old Austin state representative overcame a 4-1 spending disparity and will become the first Latina governor of Texas. The Texas Republican Party hadn’t lost a gubernatorial election since 1990. For the Texas commercial real estate industry, all eyes will likely turn to Hinojosa’s plan for a data center development moratorium , as well as stricter regulations on water and power usage and an end to tax breaks for the industry. Texas has more data centers under development than any other state, and it rose in the ranks to the top data center market this year, surpassing Virginia. Talarico has also called for tighter data center regulations and said their construction shouldn’t contribute to the state’s affordability crisis . While the Republican candidates had also called for the end of tax breaks and stricter regulations for data center development, their plans differed at the granular level. Talarico’s defeat of the Republican Senate nominee, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton , will make him the state’s first Democratic senator since 1988, before the 37-year-old Talarico was born. Talarico had 4.7 million votes , or about 55%, to Paxton’s 3.7 million late Tuesday night. Paxton, who defeated incumbent John Cornyn in the primary election, faced controversies like his 2023 impeachment and high-profile members of his party refusing to back him . More than a third of the impeachment articles involved Paxton’s relationship with embattled Austin real estate developer Nate Paul . Paxton also has a significant real estate portfolio that is at issue in his ongoing divorce. items.description: Dunleer Trades Huntington Beach Industrial in Off-Market Sale Dunleer, a Los Angeles-based private real estate investment and development firm, closed the $8.23-million sale of Talbert Industrial Park, a newly renovated, two-building small-bay industrial property located at 7602 Talbert Ave. in Huntington Beach. With an average annual household income above $145,000 within a five-mile radius, it’s one of Southern California’s most desirable multi-tenant industrial locations.” Carter Hadley and Alexander Harrold of Matthews Real Estate Investment Services represented Dunleer. The buyer was a private investor based in San Diego. items.description: Core, Midloch Acquire Celebrated Denver Shopping Center Core Acquisitions and Midloch Investment Partners⁠ purchased the 271,632-square-foot Lamar Station Plaza property on Wednesday for $30.25 million. The Denver Business Journal reports that the center is home to Casa Bonita, a famed eatery that attracts more than 650,000 visits a year. Other tenants at the center include Planet Fitness⁠, Ross Dress for Less⁠, Dollar Tree, Dutch Bros coffee and Arc Thrift Stores, alongside other local restaurant, service and specialty tenants. Core plans to make improvements such as roof replacements and upgrades to the facade. Cushman & Wakefield the sale to Core Acquisitions and Midloch Investment.
